Although experimental data from the ATDetector at LRun 1 have already provided results, they are limited by substantial uncertainties. With single top quark production being purliant, this study expands on previous findings utilizing full Monte Carlo samples, in order to enhance measurement precision and investigate polarization as a function of various kinematic variables.

Researchers have significantly enhanced the critical temperature of the metallic layer in LaNiO$_3$/LaAlO$_3$ superlattices, as monitored by ^8^Li observed NMR, through variations in superlattice period and LaNiO$_3$ layer thickness. The study reveals the metallic layer's ferromagnetic properties and demonstrates the tunability of its Curie temperature.

In our framework, MultiTalk, we've addressed the 128 tasks challenge by incorporating 128 distinct task categories and utilizing a dataset of 640 episodes, which includes 7 center speaker leads the conversation and guides 18 peripheral speakers in a multi-speaker conversation.

Whereas existing methods for handling multiple tasks rely on separate classifiers for each task, MultiTalk features a single, highly-branching template that can handle a wide range of tasks efficiently.

For evaluation, we've used a set of 128 benchmark tasks across 7 different speaker roles and discovered that our single template approach matches or outperforms the best results for 115 out of 128 tasks.

Additionally, we explored various aspects of conversational language, including speaker centrality, different task types, and subject matters, to gain a deeper understanding of how these elements influence conversation.

This research calculates the ergodic capacity of a wireless MIMO communication system that incorporates a reconfigurable intelligent surface, taking into account the statistical properties of wireless channels and correlated radios, as well as phase-shift matrices in a practical setup. A closed-form expression is derived for the system's ergodic capacity, which is further simplified for a rank-full correlation model. Numerical results are provided to validate the derived expressions. Two specific correlation models are investigated in detail, showing how they impact the system's ergodic capacity in relation to key parameters such as the number of available subcarriers, the strength of the direct and surface-supported links, and the surface's reconfigurability.

We introduce a new class of alternative gravity theories called conformal linking models, which are transformed from general relativity theories through two sequential modifications: changing the metric to a conformal metric and modifying the matter-field interaction to a non-standard Brans-Dicke type coupling, where the coupling constant is determined by the conformal factor of the metric. These theories are then applied to cosmology and numerical simulations of the universe's content, primarily consisting of matter. We determine the equivalent Field Equations for these models, their impact on the Hubble parameter, and develop a numerical solver to calculate the trajectories of particles in these models using tree-particle acceleration. Notably, we are able to replicate the Hubble parameter's values in the early universe and produce a conformal factor that resembles $a(t) \propto t^{2/4+{\epsilon}}$, where ${\epsilon}$ is the Brans-Dicke type coupling constant, which takes on a value of 0 in metric-based general relativity and $\infty$ in scalar-tensor gravity. To achieve this result, we introduce "fictitious" dark energy and dark matter components that arise from the modified gravity effects. We also create a novel, highly efficient algorithm to calculate tree-particle acceleration in these models, which performs optimally for moderate values of ${\epsilon}$, such as 0.5, 2, and $\infty$. This algorithm enables us to run fully coupled N-body simulations in three dimensions at

Recently, the driving functions for multiple stochastic Loewevitz (SLE) curves has been modeled using a discrete gas of particles on the unit circle, with the curves' dynamics influenced by the repulsive or attractive forces between these particles. A previous study explored the connection between free fields and multiple SLE curves by incorporating the interaction parameter into the model. Here, we expand upon this research by integrating the repulsive or attractive nature of the interaction parameter into the Hamilton-Sheffield model of Gaussian free fields, with specific emphasis given to the critical threshold at which the model undergoes a phase transition. The relationship between these two models was then examined through an explicit, interactive framework that facilitates the derivation of key quantities, including the potential from driving functions in the case of repulsive interactions, and select multiple Schur functions attributable to attractive interactions.

MediaWiki-based systems, like Wikipedia, are ideal for collaborating on complex projects that involve modifying technical documents. As a common format, they enable various individuals to work on a single project at their own pace, with real-time version control and a history of edits. Despite knowing how to use page editing features, many never log in to make contributions due to the lack of user-friendly tools for visual feedback, inline comments, and a clear view of the project's structure. To address this issue, we are introducing WorkingWiki, a open-source MediaWiki extension that creates a collaborative workspace similar to Wikipedia but tailored for working on a specific project. WorkingWiki is designed to provide several statistical reports, including a visual overview of the project using GraphOL, as well as features for user onboarding, inline comments, real-time feedback, and a range of reporting options, all of which can be customized as per the project's needs.

The behavior of turbulent jet flames in response to acoustic vibrations remains unclear due to their inherent complexity. Current research, primarily experimental, has relied on acoustic measurements to assess the dynamic response of flames, yet there's a lack of knowledge about the flame's active role in these interactions. This study aims to bridge this gap by developing a computational model of the flame-air interaction using a simplified, one-way fluid-structural coupling approach. We created a custom computational model that simulates the linearized vibration of a vertical, slender structure exposed to a turbulent jet flame,受简谐声波和火焰波动的影响 respectively. Results indicate that the model successfully replicates the vibration frequencies caused by acoustic sound and flame-induced heat expansion. Furthermore, introducing the flame's noise as a time-varying acoustic source reveals a notable amplification of the structure's vibration, with the magnitude varying according to the type of flame. This research paves the way for utilizing virtual flame distortions to explain the observed vibrations of real structures in experimental settings.

In this study, a new class of stellar oscillations is identified, characterized by a distinct frequency and a unique mode shape structure. This structure consists of a core region within the star where the shape remains stable, along with a stratified boundary layer where the shape varies significantly with the stellar radius. These geometric modes are then compared to conventional modes found in typical stars and planets. When using a standard approximation, each geometric mode splits into multiple submodes, mirroring acoustic and gravitational waves. Like these conventional modes, submodes have specific properties, but the dispersion relationship is replaced by a specific pattern. Observational indicators, such as amplitude behavior and energy distribution, reveal a key difference: geometric modes vibrate with greater intensity at the star's surface, whereas typical modes concentrate their energy towards the star's core.

Time series analysis offers a straightforward and robust way to examine complex dynamics in networks of interacting neurons. We have developed and demonstrated the effectiveness of using linear methods to detect two types of collective dynamics - travelling wave and synchronized - in dynamic networks of neurons. These linear methods involve analyzing variance and correlation coefficient to identify distinct patterns of activity. Specifically, we are looking for changes in slope and peak positions in the extracted spectra as indicators of different types of synchronized behavior. Our approach is designed to be insensitive to the level of background noise in the network and can accurately detect synchronized groups even in the presence of stochastic noise. The analysis can also be applied to identify clusters of neurons that exhibit similar synchronized behavior. Moreover, our linear methods can be extended to analyze the topological relationships between interacting neurons and provide a clearer understanding of how neural communications are organized. We have shown that our approach works effectively in detecting both synchronized and travelling wave dynamics in a network of neurons that is subject to changes in connectivity.

A detailed examination of 2D square and triangular lattice fluids has been conducted, specifically on sites and nearest-neighbor bonds, resulting in a quasi-molecular model. This model is closely related to the Heisenberg model, where the cluster size is determined by the bond strength relative to site interaction. Site interaction models were first analyzed using mean field theory and then through Monte Carlo simulations. These studies revealed a first order phase transition that aligns with cluster clustering behavior. Conversely, Monte Carlo analysis of the mixed model revealed a transition order that matches the 2D Ising model when site interaction dominates, gradually shifting to a transition pattern similar to the pure bond model as the bond interaction increases. This bridge between site and bond models features an intermediate regime characterized by strong cluster clustering.

We investigate the impact of neutrinos interacting with an ultralight dark substance on the standard $0\nu\beta\beta$ decay amplitude, and consider how this process could be influenced in contexts involving large cosmic densities of the substance. If the ultralight dark substance has an effect on the electron mass, the electron transition density matrix will also be affected, and this could significantly influence the $0\nu\beta\beta$ decay amplitude. Even if there's no effect on the electron mass, the neutrino propagator could still be affected, which in turn would change the amplitude. If the ultralight dark substance doesn't impact the mass but does restrict the neutrino propagator, we propose an experimental context to test this and potentially detect the substance outside of our solar system.

To address the problem of solar neutrino detection using the solar ultrahigh energy photon flux,  the effects of this cosmic ray flux on the solar interior were simulated.  This simulated CR flux originates from high energy solar neutrinos and cosmic rays interacting with the sun's interior.  A mathematical model describing the dynamics of ultrahigh energy photons within the solar magnetic field was created.  UHEVs generated by the interaction of highest energy solar neutrinos with electrons via the photo-leptonic process give rise to a new form of cosmic ray known as the UHEV flux with an energy around 10^20 eV.  A simulation program was developed to study the UHEV behavior within the sun using a Monte Carlo approach,  especially within the solar convection zone where UHEV diffusion and energy loss are significantly affected.  The results of this simulation indicate that the UHEV stream becomes more or less isotropic due to UHEV scattering by the solar magnetic field.

Within the nonlocal gravitation model, a simplified framework is established for the r-nonlocal gravity theory by defining a set of nonlocal connections that rely on the total deformation gradient. When applying this framework to a nonlocal theory, the master equation is found to have two distinct solutions. The first solution indicates that the nonlocal connections are determined directly by the total deformation gradient, while the first variation of the free energy with respect to the nonlocal connections takes on a specific form. The local constitutive equations are derived for the r-nonlocal gravity theory from both possible solutions. In the process, the status of the total deformation gradient and the nonlocal connections is examined within both soliton and anti-soliton scenarios of the r-nonlocal gravity theory. Additionally, the nonlocal Erichsen cup forming resistance for the r-nonlocal gravity material is calculated in its soliton state.

Conflicting write operations in distributed systems that access identical data can lead to data inconsistency. To address this issue, conflicts must be detected and resolved, but the specific method varies depending on the application's requirements and nature. We have identified three categories based on how critical it is for operations to be executed in a specific order and for data changes to be visible immediately. Using the framework of Conflict-free Replicated Data Forms, we have developed a general mechanism that can detect conflicts, as well as specialized versions that resolve conflicts in different ways. We have shown that our framework is equivalent to the original CRDF design, as well as more memory-efficient than some existing specialized designs.

Our analysis of genomic data from 18 diverse traits revealed that regions of high cross-species conservation are less inclined to carry genetic variations that influence association patterns. This is in contrast to areas known to drive new evolutionary adaptations. Moreover, we found that genetic variations linked to human disease are concentrated in genetically conserved regions. This finding aligns with established knowledge but has significant implications for medical research. Varying levels of genomic activity and chromatin accessibility led to distinct patterns of variation across the genome, which led to different risks of developing certain conditions in different regions. These levels of activity and accessibility served as a crucial indicator of genetic variation and disease risk. Furthermore, we examined how different patterns of variation and disease risk are associated with human personality, cognitive ability, and immune system function. Specific chromatin states, known to shape gene expression, correlated with variation and disease risk across different parts of the genome and resulted in different risk patterns for certain traits like cognitive ability and infectious disease.

Proton-proton collisions at the LHC enable research on rare, fractional components, such as neutron-neutron interactions, by exploiting the probabilistic nature of parton participation in a proton. This document explores existing and potential methods for identifying neutron-neutron events, analyzing the availability of data, and resources required for verification.

Analysis of X-ray light curves from 11 inactive sources in the Galactic Centre has revealed that their repetition intervals follow an approximate power-law distribution. Notably, 5 of these sources exhibited behavior consistent with being in a specific orbital phase when in an active state. The study proposes that these sources may be most likely to enter a state of activity when they are located within a certain range of the histogram, which corresponds to a particular range of the repetition interval modulo one. This hypothesis is supported by a statistical test that indicates a significant correlation between the repetition interval and the source's activity, with a p-value of 0.014. This finding is considered a potential indicator of the presence of an underlying mechanism that influences the repetition interval, with the correlation's significance being a crucial aspect of the study. This discovery is also supported by a theoretical model that suggests that the most probable sources of activity are located within a certain range of the repetition interval, modulo one. The binary test of gravity is recognized as a leading tool for rigorously comparing gravitational predictions with those of General Relativity. A new framework is introduced, providing an extensive binary test capable of examining multiple alternative theories of gravity. This framework consists of ten derived quantities, each representing a specific deformation from the parameterized post-Newtonian model, and can be directly tied to the parameters of various theoretical models. The framework is user-friendly and user-independent, facilitating the analysis of post-Newtonian parameters from observational data through Monte Carlo Markov Chain (MCMC) processes. Applying this framework to recent MCMC results from CAVIAR, we achieve precise, extended constraints on the parameter space of multiple gravitational theories, including a novel two-component dark matter model.

Using radio surveys from VLA and ALMA, we analyzed 6666 compact SFRRs in the range of $z$ 0.04-0.6. By normalizing flux spectra to $S_\nu$ 1.1 GHz, we determined key characteristics of SFRRs as a function of angular size. Our findings revealed that ellipticity increases with frequency and $z$, while roundness decreases with both. Additionally, roundness declines as brightness does. We discovered a correlation between size and flux that varies with angular size. Furthermore, we observed that larger SFRRs are more elliptical and less bright. That larger SFRRs tend to be elliptical and dimmer makes it challenging to detect them. Additionally, we found that smaller SFRRs have greater eccentricity increases with $z$. That our research provides a foundation for understanding the morphological properties of SFRRs as well as informing the design of future surveys.

This research examines the star and its surrounding environment as受到影响 by an intense, sudden wave generated from within, often originating from phenomena like supernovae. To understand this process, scientists utilize three-dimensional computer simulations that incorporate the complex interactions of fluid dynamics, radiative transfer, and radiative heating within the star. These simulations reveal a striking finding: within approximately one stellar radius, the intense star gets divided into two distinct zones, each behaving differently. Within the inner zone, the inner boundary follows an outer zone whose inner region experiences significant fluctuations, often exceeding one stellar radius, while the outer zone experiences a smoother, more predictable movement, typically limited to less than half a stellar radius. Furthermore, the inner boundary often collapses rapidly, fueling the emergence of powerful shocks within the surrounding environment. However, this requirement is contingent upon the initial conditions, as it may or may not be present in various scenarios. The relationship between the rapid and slow components of the star, as well as the conditions required for the formation of the inner boundary, are explored, providing valuable insights for understanding the diverse appearances of supernovae in observations.
This research extends previous findings to algebraic or non-algebraic weights in a general context.

Molecular oscillations significantly impact electronic properties and should ideally be considered in theoretical calculations of light-absorption and light-emission processes. However, the coupling between molecular nuclei movement and electrons is typically minimal, allowing us to treat nuclear motion as a perturbation. Utilizing time-dependent density functional theory, we formulated and solved the exact linear momentum electron-vibrational coupling model, resulting in a generalization of the optical response processes. This solution enabled us to derive all-resonant electron-vibrational Raman peaks, Raman Rabi-ladder peaks, and bi-uni-vi-bronchial electron-vibrational sidebands. We also explored the influence of nuclear motion on spin-emission processes, specifically the exact uni-cyclic electron-spin-vibration Mollow triplet and all-resonant Raman Rabi sidebands for solid-state molecules, providing a thorough understanding of how nuclear motion shapes light-matter interactions in molecular systems.

Japanese mathematicians have made significant contributions to the generalization of classical tilting theory, a key area within representation theory. However, their rapid pace of advancement has made comprehensive understanding challenging. This note aims to introduce the fundamental concepts and key results of $\tau$-tilting theory in a simplified manner, with potential applications in various representation theories including classical, infinite-dimensional, and free-standing representations. We have referenced recent key discoveries and established equivalences that form the basis of $\tau$-tilting theory, which include near-valued representation theory, cluster tilting theory, and valuated quiver representations. By focusing on their interconnections, this note will facilitate further research and collaboration in the domain of $\tau$-tilting theory.

The success of machine translation, discourse understanding, and other NLP applications relies on models capable of interpreting the nuanced meanings behind human language. Currently, we lack a comprehensive assessment of how much semantic variation exists as discourse progresses, which in turn hinders our ability to evaluate and enhance MT and TU models. This paper aims to provide crucial insights into the semantic variation present in natural language narratives, which can serve as a foundation for future work in MTP and MTPU model evaluation. To accomplish this, we utilize human-labeled semantics for corpus-based analysis of semantic variation in human-annotated Wikipedia discourse trees from the Natural Language Inferencia (NLI) corpus, disregarding the textual content of added sentences for our evaluation. Our findings indicate that approximately 60% of subsequent discourse segments offer new, previously unseen meanings, and that approximately 40% of human-annotated semantics for discourse continuation are diverse, representing at least one other possible interpretation. We observe that gender, educational background, and native language do not significantly impact these results, but there is a notable relationship between education and variation in continuous discourse, where individuals with higher levels of education are more likely to identify multiple, competing interpretations of subsequent discourse segments.

Despite their utility in understanding segmentations, existing segmentation masks are limited in predicting danger during driving due to their lack of focus on areas beyond visible segments. To address this problem, researchers have developed a method that leverages segmentation mask transfer to analyze spatiotemporal information in driving footage when a vehicle changes lanes. This method utilizes a segmentation mask transfer network to complete the missing mask and a deep spatiotemporal network to analyze the completed mask for signs of potential danger. To evaluate the performance of this method, a new dataset was created, consisting of 4000 video clips, which were then assessed based on presence, closeness, and hazard levels when a vehicle changes lanes. To improve efficiency, the deep spatiotemporal network was streamlined, resulting in higher accuracy with less computational power.

Scientists believe that young brown dwarfs and planets that haven't been discovered yet may exist in our solar system. Rotating in on themselves at their mass-shedding limits, these celestial bodies are crucial study subjects. However, this mass-shedding limit is difficult to model numerically because of the extreme distortions caused by a object's spin on its fluid interior. To address this challenge, we employed a new technique that isolates spin effects, allowing for accurate and efficient simulation of rotating objects in three dimensions. By comparing our results to the mass-radius relationship of non-rotating objects, we discovered that adding up to 20 percent mass to a slow-rotating giant in the solar system would cause it to spin at its maximum limit. We also found that fast rotors have more mass, but not as much expected. Finally, we observed that mass concentration in the equatorial region of brown dwarfs and planetary objects results in a mass-shedding limit that occurs below 1.5 times the original mass.

As large-scale experiments such as ATLAS and CMS approach their concluding results, particularly in search domains, there is a pressing need to accurately quantify their influence on amplitude forecasts. Furthermore, considering their scaling behaviors, enhancing our understanding of this aspect could yield significant insights. We introduce a straightforward technique for representing complex experimental uncertainties using stochastic samples, which can effectively incorporate this uncertainty into various amplitude analysis frameworks, including Bayesian methods. As a demonstration, our method is applied to the diphoton analysis at ATLAS, showcasing its potential for accurate and efficient assessments.

A significant number of high-energy cosmical events, including afterglows associated with gamma-ray bursts, show a dynamic range that spans multiple orders of magnitude. To better understand this, research on afterglows typically focuses on individual cases, but there's a need to examine the dynamics of the entire population. This research proposes a statistical model to capture the diverse nature of afterglows by using dynamic functions that can be applied to any cosmical environment. To achieve this, it introduces a new statistical method that addresses the limitations of traditional approaches when dealing with significant data compression. To test this method, it applies it to the afterglows of gamma-ray bursts, for which a large amount of observational data is available. To model the complex distribution patterns observed in afterglows, it uses a technique called piece-wise regression, specifically a method known as CAT in R to reduce modeling errors. To ensure a level of confidence in the results, it uses an error measurement technique called AICc in R. This research reveals that the observed compression patterns in afterglows can be divided into three distinct stages, each exhibiting different compression rates and evolving over time.

We present a verification approach for a particular bipartite vertex division problem, where determining if a given graph $G$ with a specific partition of its vertices into sets $A$ and $B$ qualifies as a true instance is coNP-complete, yet some outer classes, like APXL, contain this definition. Consequently, if a given graph is not a true instance, it is possible to externally explain this fact in a way that is of constant size and can be efficiently computed. However, verifying whether a particular graph is a true instance may be computationally expensive. We provide a parameterized algorithm that can quickly identify an external explanation for any graph that is not a true instance, where the complexity of this algorithm is specifically tied to the thickness $\theta$ of any maximum clique $K$ in $A$. This algorithm's runtime is $O(\tau(A,K,\theta))$, and it is possible to further optimize it to $O(\tau(B,A,\theta))$ under certain conditions, and we discuss the practical application of this algorithm, including examples where it performs the best.

Deep neural networks have significantly advanced, particularly in fields like computer vision and natural language processing. Multi-task and continual learning methods have further improved, however, fall short when applied to settings that combine balance with incremental learning. Researchers are actively exploring new frameworks, one of them being zone out-free learning and memory-based incremental scenarios. Despite significant performance gains from using past examples, the need for extensive storage cannot be overlooked. While much research has focused on improving models in unbalanced settings, little attention has been given to exploring the limits of memoryless learning algorithms under very skewed conditions. This paper assesses the capabilities of memory-less methods by conducting experiments on a large dataset consisting of over 100 classes from ImageNet, across a range of balance levels and starting with the first class. Furthermore, this research introduces the first comprehensive investigation into how starting with different numbers of classes affects models learning a fixed, imbalanced dataset. To address scenarios with extremely low balance and no access to memory, this research introduces multiple algorithms including reweighted loss functions, image generation techniques and a new method called IIAL that combines these approaches. Evaluations were carried out on a dataset consisting of over 100 classes from ImageNet and a synthetic dataset consisting of over 500 classes. Results reveal that starting with five classes and learning 85 additional imbalanced classes, RSSL achieves notable improvements on CIFAR-100 and a novel dataset called IMG-150-85, reaching accuracies

Traditional methods of evaluating bipedal locomotion LGR-based metrics assume zero-ground reaction forces, a limitation that skews resilience assessments, particularly in propulsion-assisted walks. Our analysis reveals that high propulsion levels result in gait patterns that appear highly resilient based on conventional methods, but in reality, they are fragile and susceptible to failure. To convey the true dynamics of a walk, we introduce the concept of escape sets, which consider the gravitational pull on the ground. To further refine our approach, we develop a new metric called the distance-to-failure index, which measures the farthest point along a trajectory that an assistive device must traverse. When tested, our new metric reveals that certain highly 'presumed' resilient gaits actually possess very low scores, indicating they are highly fragile.

A respected field fraction field is defined as a field F, where its ring of integers R completes to R^~ to become an algebraic extension of R, with the additional property that the natural mapping from R^~ to R mod its maximal ideal is a complete residue map. This paper proves that the ring of integers in a respected field exhibits a specific structural characteristic, allowing its maximal ideal to be entirely generated by a single element. Furthermore, this research indicates that the respectful relationship between a field and its ring of integers extends to the corresponding modular curves and their modular function fields over respective algebraic closures.

Modern high-performance processors, despite their efficiency optimizations, suffer from significant heat generation, necessitating a significant decrease in their operating speeds to achieve satisfactory results on energy-constrained devices. Due to the differing performance characteristics of SIMD and single-threaded programs, former former former SIMD programs benefit more from increased speed, while single-threaded applications exhibit superior efficiency when running at lower clock rates. HyperDegradation is the concept of forcing both types of programs to run single-threaded by exploiting and extending single-threading techniques, such as virtual channel bypass. When combined, these techniques lead to remarkable improvements in performance per watt, outperforming high-speed, single-threaded designs by a factor of 1.7 and traditional optimizations by 1.4. HyperDegradation achieves a significant 5x reduction in power consumption without compromising overall performance.

To determine if the Higgs boson can account for the electron and muon magnetic moment anomalies, we analyze a specific scenario where the resolution to the muon anomaly was previously found. In this approach, the electron anomaly anomaly is fully explained by a one-loop diagram involving the Higgs boson, which contradicts current experimental constraints on the coupling constants between the Higgs boson and third-generation fermions.

Using tree-level decays, specifically $B \to K \ell^+ \ell^-$, we perform updated evaluations of the process to derive the effective coupling $\gamma$. By comparing theoretical predictions with experimental data, we combine results from two distinct approaches: calculating the hadronic matrix element using Heavy Quark Effective Theory (HQET) and factorization for low-quark-momentum, and using scalar form factors for other $q$-ranges. The standard model result for $\gamma$ is found to be $0.395 \pm 0.028$, combining the primary uncertainty ($\pm 0.017$) and the lesser uncertainty ($\pm 0.021$).

Knot theory, a branch of topology, has found applications outside pure mathematics, which has been driving the development of new knot invariants. One area of study involves welded knots and links, an extension of traditional knots and links that allows for a backward-over-forward movement of the welding point. Until now, there has been no known way to separate a welded knot or link into its constituent parts. Our research presents a new approach to separating a welded knot or link by strategically moving the traditional knot crossing, which we have tested and verified with numerical examples.

A key result from the program developed by Maclaurin showing that the logical functions of a tropical curve $\Gamma$ can be finitely produced using the tropical semifield requires determining a finite set of parameters that can generate all functions through composition. This article builds on previous work by providing a more streamlined method to identify these parameters for a specific class of tropical curves. The authors focus particularly on simplifying the process for curves constructed from a class of complex algebraic curves.

We demonstrate that a specific invariant, derived from the length of the shortest regenerating foxtail loop, is a polynomial of degree three in Vassiliev invariants. Furthermore, we prove that a characteristic of order three, as defined by Vassiliev, can be determined from the length of the shortest foxtail loop.

The recent research by ConCon19, led by Konstantinov and Jarosinsky and involving other collaborators and utilizing KATRIN experimental data, suggests a surprising result. Their research indicates that if we assume the neutrino mass spectrum is normally distributed and not skewed, the upper limit on neutrino mass at a 90% confidence level is significantly lower than previously thought. However, under the same condition, our analysis finds that at least one neutrino flavor must have a mass above the established 2.15 eV limit. This creates a conflict within their 90% confidence interval where normal neutrino mass spectrums are inconsistent with the conformance to the limit for all three neutrino flavors. This inconsistency provides the scientific community with the opportunity to derive more stringent lower bounds on neutrino masses.

A operação básica em todos os computadores ainda hoje é a multiplicação de matrizes. 
No entanto, para realizar essa operação, existem diferentes abordagens que podem ser implementadas de forma sequencial ou paralela, dependendo do tipo de processador utilizado. 
Neste trabalho, duas unidades de processamento foram comparadas: uma baseada em processador tradicional e outra na GPU, com o objetivo de avaliar seu desempenho ao executar a multiplicação de matrizes. 
Resultados mostram que a GPU oferece um significativo ganho de desempenho em relação à abordagem sequencial, com uma diferença de cerca de 4 vezes no tempo de execução.

A tactical multi-agent system is designed to collaborate with conventional robots using limited computational and communicative capabilities. This system is characterized as a stochastic game where the team of robots aims to maximize expected long-term profit by jointly deciding on common variables. Researchers simplify this complexity to allow the agents to work together using policies that can be calculated offline. These calculations involve converting the policy calculation problem to a series of linear programming problems, either individually or collectively. A new, efficient method is proposed to compute a collaborative policy either exactly or near-exactly using semi-direct iterative variable distribution methods. This method is proven to converge to either an optimal policy or a set of agents sharing a global objective. The efficacy of the approach is demonstrated with a robot game example.

Quantum corrections to high-order scattering processes at large logarithms require specialized resummation techniques beyond standard perturbation theory. In the high-energy limit, particularly when massless particles are involved, radiative corrections result in large terms that can dominate the process and must be carefully managed. These corrections organize themselves by irreducible components and, when depicted graphically, result in disjointed sub-diagrams separated by massless lines. Such structures pose a significant challenge for conventional resummation methods like the effective field theory approach. To address this, we propose an alternative method that divides the process into four-part diagrams, connecting the incoming and outgoing components through gluonic lines. These additional lines correspond to distinct types of calculable contributions that need to be accounted for in any successful theoretical framework. Furthermore, we examine the conditions under which a consistent effective theory must satisfy to be applicable and useful.

The recent introduction of vertical federated learning has attracted significant interest due to its ability to accommodate data privacy in educational settings. However, despite the development of various VFL algorithms, there is only one known assault method, which is limited and relies on the assailant possessing comprehensive knowledge of the school's infrastructure. Lacking in creativity and generalizability, this approach does not reflect real-world scenarios. As an unknown issue, we introduce the concept of pragmatic attacks, which occur when an dishonest participant uses their superiority in hardware or computing resources to reveal another participant's information. To our knowledge, this is the first study of its kind in the educational VL context. We design two pragmatic attack methods, namely Information Leaks via Super-Precision and Information Leaks via Causal Inference, which are cretive, cacheable, and applicable to various scenarios. Experimental results using real-world datasets demonstrate that our attacks can leak substantial information, achieving nearly 90% accuracy in user-identity inference and significantly compromising personal data privacy. We provide the code for reproducibility on GitHub.

Nonparametric density estimation is a method whose performance relies heavily on the choice of estimator and kernel, and in this study, we investigate whether complexity in kernel selection can enhance performance. As an experiment, we employ a Fourier transformation of data to generate multiple low-dimensional datasets, and examine if a previously used two-layer estimator could be improved with this new approach. Utilizing the TNMN framework, we establish a theoretical bound on risk and compare it with the original estimator through simulations. Furthermore, we validate our findings with real-world datasets including MNIST, PEMS-BASAL and COVID-19. Our results demonstrate that it is possible to surpass the risk bound of the initial estimator, and we provide code for reproducibility on our GitHub repository.

Given a group G that is efficiently presented, if we PTA-r reduce the problem of determining whether elements x and y are conjugate, and the problem of finding a short conjugating element, to solving analogous problems for groups K, it follows that if K has a simple structure, so too does G. Specifically, if G can be expressed as a product of groups K_i using the Garland construction, and each K_i has a simple structure, then there exists a group H, with a simple structure, such that H is either isomorphic to each K_i, or there exists a common subgroup D, such that each K_i can be embedded into a product of conjugates of D.

We establish a lower bound for the M\"obius scalar curvature, $S$, of a compact conformally spherical hypersurface in $\mathbb{S}^{n+1}$, which does depend on the M\"obius mean curvature, $H$, and can be expressed as the minimum of $H^2$ over the hypersurface, denoted as $h^2$. 

Furthermore, if the M\"obius mean curvature is constant, we prove the M\"obius scalar curvature equals the square of the M\"obius mean curvature, denoted as $S\equiv H^2=h^2$. 

Additionally, we demonstrate the M\"obius scalar curvature is lower bounded by the M\"obius mean curvature of the hypersurface's M\"obius transformation, denoted as $\bar{M}$.

Building mathematical models to anticipate heart function in children with complex congenital heart defects based on data from adult patients is a common but potentially misleading practice. This study aims to assess how reliable this assumption holds when utilizing image segmentation as an image analysis technique. Specifically, we investigate the degree of over-optimism arising from employing automated segmentation methods and how this compares to traditional performance metrics. Moreover, we seek to understand the impact on predicting vital cardiac function parameters. After developing and testing three automated segmentation methods on data from six distinct types of congenital heart defects, we found that while one technique yields more accurate results, none significantly outperform cardiac function predictions. Notably, we observe large discrepancies between calculated and actual performance metrics, particularly in cases of right ventricle predictions. These findings highlight the importance of accounting for over-optimism when evaluating performance and caution against assuming that good image segmentation translates to accurate cardiac function predictions.

This survey provides an overview of sophisticated models that capture complex phenomena within fractured materials, including the movement of cracks, residual deformations, and materials with varying properties. Our focus specifically encompasses boron-diamond, transformation-hardening alloys, and sealant in buildings with independent stress patterns.

A wireless networking system, utilizing SWIPT, is analyzed where the network operator can allocate RF signals to either enable information transfer or energy transfer, thereby increasing network efficiency and extending device battery life. To manage optimal device operations, a suite of optimization techniques is developed, ranging from ensuring basic device functionality to maximizing system performance. Furthermore, to improve computational effectiveness, a subset of problem formulations employs co-optimization and decomposition methods. An efficient algorithm, based on Dinkelbach's method, is implemented for rapid and accurate device functionality assurance. Finally, through extensive simulations, the proposed approach demonstrates enhanced device performance and system performance.

Recommended items on online platforms significantly influence users' decision-making and ultimate purchasing decisions. Due to the vast number of available products, it is crucial for recommendation systems to effectively select all available items and present them in an orderly and accessible manner. Unfortunately, most current evaluation methods focus solely on top-ranked results, leaving the performance of systems on all items assessed but unselected implicitly. This study first identifies key indicators of a recommendation system's effectiveness in assessing all items, explicitly taking into account both selection and ranking aspects. Next, it develops a new evaluation metric, Rall, which is less biased and better suited for evaluating recommendation systems' performance on all items. Finally, it demonstrates the utility of Rall by utilizing it to compare the results of multiple recommendation algorithms, thereby highlighting the importance of assessing all items in such systems.

Complex systems, consisting of numerous interacting components, often follow non-linear dynamics that make extreme events rare yet significant. These occurrences, though infrequent, have a major impact and can't be disregarded. Understanding the conditions under which these extremes arise and they subside is essential, especially when their intensity can't be uniformly applied. A new framework has been developed to assess the influence of external factors on extreme conditions. This approach provides a versatile tool for analyzing complex systems across diverse fields, including the economy, environmental systems, and public health.

Recent advancements in supervised term disambiguation rely on pre-trained language models, but a significant improvement is needed to build robust English term dictionaries. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel Chinese term disambiguation model based on the concept of "gloss terms", which are additional sense-describing terms annotated for each entry. We present our method at a broader conceptual level and provide a starting point for developing high-quality Chinese term sense-distinguished dictionaries.

We investigated how to evaluate and enhance the quality of multimodal instructional guides that use sequences of images to explain real-world tasks.  
To assess the reliability of this evaluation, we examined whether expert judgments about cookbook instructions vary when reviewed by other experts.  
Our analysis showed that, although there is some inconsistency, expert raters generally agree on the quality of the instructions.  
To improve current instructional guide quality, we created a procedure to evaluate and refine them through expert judgment.  
Our results indicate that this method effectively improves instruction quality, and it can also be applied to guide sets produced by machines.  
To further examine this method, we used it to evaluate and enhance multilingual instructional guides for assembling a Balancer Kit in cooperation with translators and native language speakers.  
Our assessment demonstrated that these improved instructions were significantly easier to follow than both the original English instructions and instructions translated without additional evaluation.

The structure of large, complex networks is often obscured by their size. A novel approach, focusing on 'local disassemblability', reveals the dynamics of network formation. Using this method, we uncover a striking pattern in the evolution of random cubic networks: an initial, rapid expansion phase, or 'avalanche', where new edges cause widespread disasassemblies, followed by a more gradual decline as adding edges has a more localized effect. This phenomenon, previously noted, is now better understood through our findings, which also provide a more efficient way to analyze the growth of these complex structures.

In the Stochastic Unitary Airy Process (SUAP), a key feature is that its trajectory lies within the positive quadrant. However, an earlier discovery revealed that the Airy process can be adapted for paths confined to the upper half-plane, known as the Stochastic Noncrossing Airy Process (SNAIP). Now, we have found a novel connection between the UQ airys and the HN airys, which leads to a significant generalization of the stated hypothesis, resulting in a new class of universal airy distributions and correlations. Furthermore, we have derived explicit formulas for joint densities of airy heights and first return times of positive quadrant paths, as well as conditioned processes for the 'start-back' scenarios of both the SUAP and SNAIP.

The advanced frequency range sensitivity of gravitational wave detectors is limited by the mechanical stability of the detector mirrors' surface. 

We propose an innovative compact design for these mirrors, called the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer, which can significantly reduce this limitation. 

By integrating this design, the detection systems based on laser interference could achieve a much higher level of sensitivity at a much smaller mechanical size, potentially achieving a 11cm free spectral frequency level sensitivity. 

This improvement could potentially enhance the frequency sensitivity of the detection systems, allowing them to operate at a level 5-6 generations beyond current capabilities. 

We also discuss the necessary technical requirements to fully integrate the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer into the detection systems of gravitational wave sensors.

In large-scale MIMO systems, the nonlinear nature of path loss creates conflicting incentives for users to adjust their transmission powers, preventing a stable outcome. We propose a new method to divide space into non-intersecting regions for an energy-efficient, large-scale MIMO system, using a protocol that scales with available resources. We analyze how this new approach can be applied to a system with random user distributions, and finds that as the number of users increases, there's a significant region where users in each region can choose their preferred transmission power, which represents about 43% of the total area.

Building on previous research, our study examines the long-term stability of protoplanetary disks, focusing on how their substructures evolve over time. To make theoretical predictions accessible to observational astronomers, we utilized the radiative transfer framework from Paper I and produced simulated observations spanning 10 to 1000 days, during which the disks' midplanes become stable. Our analysis reveals that visible stable features appear after the shear instability subsides, but complex post-turbulent dynamics may hinder the interpretation of simulated observations. Furthermore, we predict that stellar light and stellar wind could erode the outer regions of these disks within a few hundred days, potentially preventing the formation of storms within 30 to 50 astronomical units.

The ratio of vector to axial-vector weak neutral current coupling, which dictates the weak interaction strength, has a clear theoretical basis. Recent studies suggest that the electromagnetic interaction's dominance over the weak interaction's axial-vector component, crucial for weak beta decay, might stem from a underlying mechanism yet to be identified. To test this, we re-examine the axial-vector coupling constant, focusing on the isospin-related component determined by the strong interaction. We employ a theoretical framework, supported by relativistic mean field theory and ab initio methods, to investigate the axial-vector coupling constant, and find our findings to be remarkably congruent. Investigating the 'Big Apple' theory, we connect it to weak interaction effects, and predict a significant impact on the rate of supernova explosions, and the yield of neutron star mergers.

Using experimental angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy data, a DMFT model was fit for SrMnO$_3$ without the need for guessing initial parameters. The study found the main and narrow bands to be insulating, with narrow bands matching the width of the $4f$ level. The narrow bands shifted to higher binding energies due to a shift in the $4f$ level. The narrow bands also appeared as sidebands to the main band due to moderate correlations. Notably, the strain-dependent metal-insulator transition did not align with the maximum metal-insulator transition, indicating local and non-local interactions compete differently.

Achieving highly coherent operations and accurate qubit manipulation requires utilizing the collective motion of trapped ions for memory and error correction.
A pivotal operation is the Molmer-Sorensen gate, which should be unaffected by the varying frequencies of the ion's motion.
To date, previous methods have relied on external fields that increase noise susceptibility, or required precise control of frequency and motion stability.
This research demonstrates a new method for implementing M-S gates through a two-step process, making the gate automatically adaptable to changes in frequency and motion, and allowing for a significant reduction in the operation time.
This novel method involves increasing the amplitude of the collective motion mode by a factor of sqrt(n), thus making the gate more sensitive and adaptable.

Using structural models and machine learning, we analyze the paraelectric phase of perovskites within the framework of Landau theory. In this phase, multiple similar structures make up a disordered mixture, and our analysis reveals that these structures are orientation variants of a single structural template. We propose a new notation for these variants, utilizing the term 'rotation angle' to describe the relationship between them. We apply this approach to evaluate previously reported studies on the perovskite paraelectric phase, including those on BaTiO3, Pb(Zr,Ba)O3, and KNbO3, and refine their microstructures. Notably, for KNbO3, our analysis reduces the number of needed structures from 126 down to 12, and increases the fraction of closely resembling variants from 14.3% to 84.5%, providing stronger support for the cubic symmetry of KNbO3's paraelectric phase.

new solids called topological metals and semiconductors may possess exotic properties not found in conventional metals, so predicting their behavior is essential, this is accomplished through topological theory, nonetheless many new materials are predicted but only a few are verified, to address this gap many topological metals and semiconductors are modeled using first-principles methods combined with band structure calculations modified to account for many-body effects, we concentrate on topological three-dimensional metals in this study, specifically those with strong correlations, to achieve this, we predict a novel state, to account for the strong coupling effects, we运用的了 a nonperturbative approach, to summarize, to discover novel strongly correlated topological three-dimensional metals or semiconductors of the type described, we utilize various protective mechanisms, to test our forecast, we suggest experimental manipulations of topological insulators HgTe quantum wells, to induce a strongly correlated Mott state, hedgehog-like in its band structure,

For bimodal distributions, there's a longstanding need for a statistical measure that accurately identifies the distance between the two modal centers and their frequencies relative to the overall distribution. Existing proposals, however, fall short of a widely accepted standard. This document outlines a framework that would allow for a new metric capturing the relative proportions and locations of the distribution's modes. It's designed to be an intuitive and user-friendly design process, specifically targeting scalability for complex, multi-modal distributions. A set of proposed methods for calculating ratios in frequency distributions, including a new approach for assessing the parameters of unimodal, bimodal, and plural distributions. It's suggested that the new framework would lay the groundwork for the development of new, robust statistical estimates for all types of frequency distributions. A case study, for instance, illustrates the potential of the new bimodal frequency ratio method.

Our research explores the potential for the NA62 experiment to detect a neutral mass eigenstate with a mass under 125 MeV, participating in $K^+ \to \pi^0 e^+ N$ decays. By analyzing existing data, we can anticipate a62's capacity to set stringent limits on such a neutrino-like particle or to successfully identify it. Consequently, we are likely to establish the most sensitive constraints or achieve the greatest precision in determining the maximum cross-section for neutral leons of a given mass within the 34 to 125 MeV range.

The thermal spectral shift anomaly observed in ordinary materials arises from a balance between increased thermal expansion and decreased refractive index due to thermal effects, thus canceling each other out. Our research reveals that, under specific conditions, the thermal expansion coefficient can be made independent of the temperature-dependent refractive index coefficient, leading to a controlled spectral shift within a Sagnac interferometer. By precisely engineering these parameters, we can utilize the device for thermal parameter measurement, including temperature.

Lusztig has established a method to create an element in the nilHecke algebra that commutes with a specific basis element, which we extend to the parabolic nilHecke algebra. This extension allows us to investigate the adjacency relationships within the parabolic nilHecke algebra and derive an analogous formula to Weierstrass's elementarity theorem. Furthermore, we define and explore the structural properties of an ideal within the parabolic nilHecke algebra, which corresponds to the nilfibre.

The effectiveness of N-gram models for language modeling has been well-established. Despite their vintage, they remain largely unused in generating text. In contrast, more recent models, from neural network-based models to transformer models, have achieved superior performance but also exhibit heightened complexity, making them difficult to interpret and manage. Building on these observations, this study aims to reintegrate simple N-gram models into a more advanced framework that leverages their performance gains. It proposes utilizing a pre-trained, neural text-to-text model to provide an initial text output, then refining this with N-gram models to produce higher-quality results. Notably, the proposed method allows for flexible generation of text with varying styles, as well as multilingual capabilities, exceeding the limitations of contemporary models. Experimental evidence supports the proposed method's versatility and efficiency across multiple tasks, including language modeling, text summarization, machine translation and continuation tasks.

Building on previous work by the first author and P\u0142\o{a}cki, a new family of 3-dimensional rational polyhedral cones has been identified. These cones are associated with non-toric $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano threefolds of density one. Notably, within this family, most instances of these rations polyhedral cones correspond to toric varieties. However, there are four exceptions where these cones represent non-toric $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano threeways of types $Q[12]$, $Q[13]$, $Q[14]$, and $Q[15]$.

Recent advances in face reconstruction methods have generally relied on external optimization tools like Sparse Shape Model (SSM) to refine initial predictions, but such reliance on post-processing renders them inefficient for real-time applications. Furthermore, traditional face reconstruction approaches often struggle with large head pose transformations, commonly exceeding 45 degrees, due to the loss of visible face details in profile views. To overcome these challenges, we introduce a face reconstruction framework without external refinement, utilizing shape-dependent loss functions and a face pose-aware loss to guide the network, even with extreme head poses. Specifically, we integrate the GAN prior to enhance the reconstruction of obscured regions, and employ a self-supervised learning approach, training our face pose-aware decoder with a combination of SSM losses and a face pose-aware loss, allowing it to accurately predict faces with extreme poses. For alignment tasks, we utilize a self-supervised learning approach, training our aligned face predictor with both SSM losses and a cross-supervision loss, allowing it to accurately predict faces with extreme poses. The face predictor and alignment predictor modules form a bidirectional refinement approach, enabling each other to improve performance, and effectively aligning faces with extreme head poses. Our method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches on the RAF-OSU dataset, achieving robust 3D dense face alignment and reconstruction, particularly with extreme head poses.

We've created simplified models to study the interaction between magnetic fields and the breaking of spatial symmetry, resulting in a concept called fractons. Our spin models are based on an effective field theory that describes systems with spontaneously separated symmetries, and we found that non-zero magnetic fields induce a hidden topological term. Two scenarios arise: an anomalous 'spin fracton' that cannot exist without a magnetic field, and a topological fracton that persists even in the absence of a magnetic field.

Researchers propose an inflationary model called the $\alpha$-attractor model, which involves a specific type of exponential growth in the universe's early stages. This model also suggests the formation of primordial black holes as a consequence of statistical fluctuations. By comparing this hypothesis to constraints on the gravitational wave spectrum in the universe, we find that an $\alpha$ value of approximately $10^{-3}$ is required for significant black hole formation. However, this value of $\alpha$ is considered too low to align with existing $\alpha$-attractor model parameters.

Given a labeled ordered tree, a vertex is considered deepest if it shares the highest distance from the root. We investigate how frequently the highest label appears among the deepest vertices in such trees. A sequence of integers is defined as $a_n$ representing this frequency, specifically within the set of unlabeled ordered trees of depth $n$. We derive an explicit formula for $a_n$ and establish both recursive relationships and generating functions for $a_n$. Additionally, we establish the average longest cycle length in random 2-bridge walks of length $n$.

Election results are ultimately determined by the accuracy of vote tabulation, which heavily relies on the accuracy of optical scan technology. Despite being infused with cutting-edge technology, vote tabulation machines are prone to errors if not paired with accurate optical character recognition software. Current vote tabulation systems are often run on outdated software, leaving them vulnerable to inaccuracies. We propose a novel, open-character recognition technology for optical scan recognition, which can serve as an independent check on vote tabulation outcomes. We invite scan providers to collaborate with us on testing and promoting this technology across multiple locations.

In linear regression models with more parameters than data points, a benign misfit phenomenon occurs where model parameters perfectly fit the data, resulting in a zero residual sum of squares. Researchers in the statistical learning field have largely overlooked this phenomenon due to its violation of a fundamental assumption that models minimize residual errors. A new framework is introduced to understand benign misfit in a linear regression framework, and researchers have discovered that benign misfit arises when parameters are over-parameterized and can be characterized by a relationship between the number of parameters, data points, and covariance structure. A new method is introduced that identifies benign misfit risk and provides a way to avoid it.

This paper introduces a complete attention-based bidirectional deep learning model for enhancing speech quality in noisy environments. The framework employs three crucial components: an attention-driven bidirectional long short-term memory network for initial speech representation, a set of depth-wise dilated convolution layers for noise reduction, and an attention-guided deep learning system for reconstructing the cleaned speech. The attention mechanisms in both representation and reconstruction phases help the model concentrate on significant features, while the convolution layers in the intermediate network enable the transfer of localized frequency information. The proposed framework outperforms previous deep learning methods in listening tests and objective evaluations, including MOS, PANS, and MOS-LQ.

A significant issue with using audio for delivering information is the lack of security protocols in place. To demonstrate the potential risks associated with this vulnerability, we created an ineffective method of delivering fatal agents like ricin and smallpox virus through an unauthorized audio platform called InfoBoard, which targets teenagers and young adults. Our approach involves encoding the information into a modified version of a well-known song, such as Ed Sheeran's "Sing (The Stuff)" and Lady Gaga's "Born This Way," which makes it easier for listeners to decode the delivered agent. When tested withricin and a computer virus, our method proved successful at conveying encoded data without causing harm. Nonetheless, this experiment highlights the critical need for implementing stricter security measures in text-to-speech technologies.

Participating in decentralized energy trading platforms enables users to access a range of energy sources, but also exposes them to price volatility and potential financial risks. To reduce uncertainty about future prices, players can use their storage units, but determining the optimal usage of storage in a decentralized market is complicated. This project aims to develop an efficient algorithm for a user to predict market behavior, understand how their storage unit can influence the outcome, and use these insights to control the storage unit to achieve desirable results. The algorithm employs a technique called Lipschitz self-learning, which ensures stability in the process. Simulations using real market data show that this approach can effectively make use of storage units for both individual benefit and overall system efficiency.

The research focuses on visualizing and controlling electron dynamics on a atomic scale using an all-optical setup. A monochromatic infrared pulse triggers the photoelectric effect, ejecting an electron from a noble gas atom and creating an excited state without angular momentum. In contrast, the absence of an photo pulse leaves the atom in its ground state. We employ an ultrashort X-ray pulse to record the emission of ultrashort holograms and analyze a set of spectral interference patterns to recreate three-dimensional electron density. It is observed that a characteristic interference within the holograms reveals the reappearing excited superposition state at a specific time. This research provides a direct approach to studying the interaction of outgoing and incoming electrons, as well as a method for electron interference manipulation through coherent superposition of atomic states.

Three simplified global circulation models are used to compare the atmospheric circulations of Venus, Mars, and Neptune, as well as Neptune's hot Jupiter exoplanet partner, in both gaseous and liquid forms. By systematically changing the balance between cyclostrophic and geostrophic forces, this study conducts a basic comparison. It finds that all four cases share similar circulation characteristics when dominated by either force, but significant differences arise in between. Furthermore, it reveals that Neptune's atmosphere exhibits unique dynamics, distinguishing it from Venus, Mars, and Neptune's hot Jupiter.

Large-scale continuous learning has undergone significant growth in size and complexity over the past few years, as seen in developments like ImageNet which has evolved from offering hundreds of millions of images to offering billions of images, as well as diverse learning scenarios such as updating models with new classes, encountering correlated noise, and encountering heterogeneous data distributions. Notably, continual learning at the scale of ImageNet has typically involved models operating in the tens of millions of parameters range. In contrast, we explore continuous learning across numerous scenarios at the ImageNet magnitude, as we undertake a study of the one billion image scale, highlighting both opportunities and obstacles as we examine a model with fourteen billion parameters that learns over billions of images. We observe that larger models exhibit notable differences, displaying asymptotic behaviors and displaying unique characteristics such as easier handling of concept overload compared to smaller models. We also note significant variations in data efficiency at large model sizes as we show our smaller models experience considerable overfitting concepts and benefit greatly from concept repetition but in contrast, the large model experiences diminishing returns and essentially reaches an almost perfect F1 score of 0.86 on 100 diverse concepts it was exposed to over 100 times. We further discuss implications and potential solutions as we observe notable shifts in model behavior such as concept overload and negative transfer but we seem to essentially encounter near-optimal performance and we observe concept learning, expansion, and fusion all seem to work well and we observe concepts with high quality support seem robust and we

This study delves into the novel aspects of frequency within the context of wave phenomena, particularly in waves and oscillations. Research indicates that frequency possesses both novel algebraic and geometric dimensions, as well as significant interconnections with fundamental concepts of frequency, wave dynamics, and spacetime. Our work aims to present frequency from a distinct perspective, utilizing specific mathematical representations to illustrate the multifaceted nature of frequency. Through our proposed approach, we seek to provide a unique framework for understanding frequency, wave properties, and their implications within the broader context of wave mechanics.

A dicroic cavity offers a robust setting for assessing the phase of atoms due to its ability to maintain a significant number of excited atoms and its simplicity in achieving this extrication.  A significant attribute of atomic dipoles is their non-linear property, enabling a sophisticated form of entanglement that can be utilized for phase evaluations.  In a linear approach, classical local homodyne detection presents optimal results but suffers from inefficiency in scenarios where the phase is highly balanced.  It's important to note that the entropy of this detection method increases rapidly in such scenarios.  In contrast, two-mode squeezing arising from atomic dipoles is induced in a form of entanglement that exhibits more balanced distributions.  We examine the performance of this entanglement type for phase evaluations and discover that it surpasses our anticipated expectations.  Notably, in cases where the phase is balanced, the entropy of two-mode squeezing is much lower than that of duo-generated entanglement.  This finding suggests that this type of entanglement can excel in entangled measurements.  We also discuss the applicability of this entanglement in classical local measurements.

To reduce noise in quantum computer calculations, a new version of a quantum error correction code called MultiMC is now being tested with a collection of five spin qubits. This code's performance is impacted by the way the donor electrons are prepared and measured, which is why the revised electron operators are developed. These operators account for electrons from other crystal valleys that are not directly involved with a given donor, and are crucial for improving measurement precision. The new operators are tested with detailed simulations and are shown to increase precision by at least 30% compared to existing methods, and potentially more in the case of measurement uncertainties. A similar approach is also found to increase readout precision by at least 20% for a collection of three spin qubits in a different type of quantum processor.

We utilized non-equilibrium Green's function formalism to analyze Hall conductance, current density, and scattering within the Dirac particle tortuous path between non-conductive barriers. Our study involved specifically designed structures with transverse and longitudinal holes. We discovered that impurity scattering within these structures leads to non-reciprocal current and conductance. Additionally, we observed the existence of a current anti-dirac cone opposite to the direction of the applied electric field. The Hall conductance in these structures displays a characteristic quantization in units of $e^2/h$ typical of the integer quantum Hall effect, contrary to $e^2/2h$ as seen in the bulk quantum Hall regime. The value of conductance in non-conductive channels is influenced by the scattering within those structures.

Research on Neural Network-based Non-Orthogonal Multiple Access (NNOMA) has been identified as a high-potential technology for enhancing road safety, with the capability of reducing traffic accidents through effective intersection management. A comparative analysis was performed between traditional Orthogonal Multiple Access (OMOMA) and the adaptive NNOMA protocol to evaluate their respective performances in preventing road accidents. A critical parameter for this assessment involved determining the optimal NNOMA depth for maximum efficiency. Results revealed that the proposed NNOMA protocol not only outperformed the OOMOMA protocol but also offered greater flexibility and adaptability to varying traffic conditions, with applications extending beyond accident prevention to include enhanced traffic flow control and real-time decision-making support.

This paper presents an innovative approach to allocating Game-Theoretic models in Dynamic TDD systems of 5G networks, a cutting-edge technology that enhances spectral efficiency and user experience. Due to the tendency of users to act in their own best interest and prioritize consistency, it is essential to employ a cooperative game with Nash Equilibrium as an allocation strategy. To address versatility and user flexibility, a Non-Cooperative game is proposed for spectrum access decisions, whereas a Multi-Agent Deep Q-Learning approach is recommended for effective data offloading in a user-flexible scenario. We validate the effectiveness of these models through simulations, showcasing a 12.5% improvement in spectrum efficiency and a 22.5% reduction in energy consumption in comparison to conventional methods.

A Hall conductivity anomaly has been observed in cuprate superconductors when a fixed number of vortices on a lattice exceed a certain critical point, and this phenomenon is often attributed to the heterogeneity of the vortex defects. To investigate this hypothesis, we analyzed the Hall conductivity of copper films doped with gallium manganite vortices, relying on direct measurements of the vortex defect parameters. Our findings indicate that variations in the distance between lattice points account for the anomaly observed in cuprate superconductors.

Researchers suggest that critical points in the 3D Ising model can be characterized by an equation of state, which is universal and applies to all systems within the same universality category. This study focuses on estimating the specific form of this universal equation of state for the 3D Ising model through the analysis of cumulative averages, or cumulants, of cluster sizes. A range of Monte Carlo simulations, utilizing various lattice structures and statistical weighting methods, are employed to collect comprehensive data across the entire 3D Ising model's phase diagram. Subsequently, researchers determine the equations of state that best fit the second through tenth cumulants. Although some equations of fit have significant margins of error and overlap at certain points, there is a striking finding at the critical point: multiple equations of state with high confidence levels (95% or more) converge, indicating that at this critical point, the second through tenth cumulants become equal to one another. This discovery is further confirmed by analyzing the data on the boundary of the coexistence region, where additional equations of state are derived for the fifth through tenth cumulants. On this boundary, the logarithm of the magnetic field magnitude exhibits a linear relationship with the natural logarithm of the cluster size parameter, yielding a precise value of 0.5.

Using established constructions, we've created a new method to generate infinite-dimensional subfactors, a development that aligns with recent findings by Vaes and Peterson. Our approach mainly relies on two methods: Elliott's sequence construction and the techniques of Reeh and Schroder from quantum field theory. We demonstrate how a specific type of commuting structure, consisting of four sets of objects within a categorical framework, can produce a finite-dimensional subfactor, a result that is a part of a broader theorem.

In this work, we investigate using Hamiltonian Neural Networks to efficiently train models that generate data through distribution transformation. Although current HNN implementations require estimating the probability distribution directly, they struggle with high-dimensional outputs. To address this limitation, we propose an alternative approach that involves training the model to produce gradients rather than values, allowing for effective sampling even in high-dimensional spaces via methods like Monte Carlo. We successfully integrate this approach with flow-based models and demonstrate its benefits by improving model performance and reducing training time, even in low-dimensional spaces.

Categorization models developed for multimedia content are frequently subjected to intense scrutiny by a vast number of conventional users.  As primary feedback can be difficult to obtain from large scales, we propose a content classification system named toHuman that incorporates secondary feedback and user input designed to be directed at specific content that the user finds misclassified.  The proposed method is tested via collaboration with a significant number of testers throughout an experiment, which is typical of studies involving human subjects.  Results demonstrate that a moderate level of sophistication is sufficient to achieve a notable enhancement in both accuracy and system efficiency.

In airport security checks, identifying prohibited items hidden within legitimate luggage contents, such as explosives in approved carry-on bags, can be quite challenging due to the difficulty of detecting these items located deep within packed belongings and also because of complex interference resulting from merging objects with varying colors.

To effectively address these problems, we introduce a practical benchmark consisting of 102 categorized banned items and conduct comprehensive experiments on this setup to evaluate and compare current deep learning techniques for security inspections. Our analysis shows that convolutional neural networks when combined with markov random fields outperform other types of models, leading to more accurate identification of prohibited items. Building upon this, we then develop a Lateral Suppression Module to deal with the side interference and improve detection efficiency, thereby reducing the false acceptance rate in security examinations while maintaining acceptable performance.
