collected from nearby access points. To evaluate the performance of this approach,
we utilized the MALLA2 dataset, and compared the results with alternative methods
such as TOA, RSSI-based, and RSSI propagation models. Our experiments demonstrate
that our method offers superior accuracy in range estimation, thereby improving
the quality of location-based services.

An alternative theory to the no-hair theorem of black holes, known as the hairy-theorem, is explored in this paper. According to dyson shell theory, a perfectly conducting sphere can emit and absorb radiation effectively. We calculate the equilibrium temperature of a dyson shell that surrounds a 'black star'. A neutron star with a mass of 3 solar masses and a radius of 9 km would have a temperature of 2.8K in a dyson shell with an inner radius of 27km. This model contradicts the observed characteristics of pulsars, which emit continuous waves, and challenges the fundamental principles of the no-hair theorem of black holes.

A discrepancy between guaranteed service quality and actual received service can cause significant issues for both users and service providers. Although detecting and addressing this discrepancy is crucial, it's often complicated to assess. To tackle this challenge, we investigate how to leverage peer-to-peer technology to enable the detection and identification of service level agreement breaches. Lacking widespread adoption of monitoring tools or possessing expert-level capabilities to operate them, network operators face difficulties in accurately identifying breaches. As an alternative, we propose utilizing peer-to-peer technology to create a network of volunteers who can help. Through a mathematical model, we demonstrate the feasibility of this approach and test its effectiveness using simulated data, ultimately showcasing its potential to provide breach identification results that are as accurate as those from professional monitoring systems.

Regenerative beam fragmentation instability poses a major obstacle to achieving high beam current and optimal beam quality in radio frequency linear accelerators, severely restricting their beam parameters. Traditional methods overcome this limitation by employing transverse beam current compensating coils. However, these methods are constrained as their compensating effect is heavily dependent on the beam's longitudinal configuration. Investigating this limitation, this study analyses the impact of energy recovery linacs on beam fragmentation and evaluates the influence of final gap design on suppressing the regenerative beam fragmentation instability. Simulations indicate that a specifically designed final gap significantly reduces the beam fragmentation instability, with effects comparable to those of the compensating coil method. Furthermore, such design sensitivity is sensitive to bunch train configuration, allowing notable improvements in reduction of the regenerative beam fragmentation instability.

Scattering neutrons can be effectively detected using a 3D scintillator sensor in n-gamma coincidence arrangements, with this project aiming to create such a device by incorporating high-purity silicon chips and a 3D proton-boron-phosphorus scintillator in close proximity. This sensor design minimizes neutron detection time thanks to its thin silicon gap, thus improving performance. To test and validate the n-gamma coincidence capability, neutron data will be collected using an external radioactive source, applying K-edge filtration to mitigate contaminating gamma signals. Ultimately, this device will be tested with a 50 Ci CNB source to assess its neutron cross-section precision, with initial results indicating a mean uncertainty below 1%.

As sub-millimeter-sized particles within star-forming environments warm up, their interaction with surrounding gases changes, significantly influencing how they stick together. 
Understanding this process as it varies with temperature remains largely unknown and needs further study, crucial for modeling the formation of planets.
In this investigation, we observe the impact of rising temperatures on the adhesion forces experienced by polystyrene and silica particles in the ranges of 20-1000 K, using a stylus-based force measurement technique.
Increasing temperature results in a decrease in surface roughness and a corresponding reduction in adhesion forces, leading to an eventual switch in the dominant mechanism guiding grain grain interactions. 
However, the process is affected by the material properties and surface characteristics of the particles involved. 
As a general pattern, the adhesion forces of the particles studied decline as temperatures increase, leading to a shift in the dominant mechanism guiding grain interactions. 
At extremely high temperatures, grain-grain interactions would likely turn into a grain-size dependent phenomenon, having a potential threshold of around 1 micron by 1000 K. 
Our data also indicates that, as the solar system's temperatures rose, its particles may have gone through at least two different grain-grain interaction thresholds, potentially leading to a critical point around the present-day solar system temperatures. 
This, in turn, might have a significant influence on the development of the early planetary system.

The lfda R package is designed for local Fisher discriminant analysis, an modification of the traditional Fisher's linear discriminant analysis. Unlike the traditional method, which seeks a single global discriminant direction, the local variant focuses on identifying projection directions specific to neighboring samples. To compute lfda, the local weighting scheme is applied to samples within the KNN framework. This package provides functions for discriminant examination and visualization, making it possible to assess and graphize the results of local Fisher discriminant analysis.

Learning policies that are effective in complex, high-stakes applications from a diverse range of demonstrations is a significant challenge in the field of imitation learning. To address this challenge, researchers have explored various approaches, including those that utilize nonlinear rigid constraints, barrier evading techniques, and diverse optimization methods. While individual approaches have yielded promising results, they often struggle with convergence and efficiency when dealing with optimization problems. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a new framework called Broad Learning with Adjustment, Nonlinear Rigid Constraints and Barrier Evading (BKLA), which integrates these methods into a unified Markov decision process framework. Through our method, we can achieve diverse behavior cloning performance that exceeds current state-of-the-art results, and we demonstrate the benefits of BKLA through multiple experimental trials.

To advance the computational efficiency of multi-loop scattering amplitudes in N^4SYM at nine loops, a new numerical value is required, specifically M_4^{$\mathcal{L}$}_. This study aims to contribute to that goal by presenting a verified calculation of the one-loop seven-point amplitude's central-emission vertex for two gluons. Initially expressed in a parametric form, this emission factor is being tested through an independent high-precision numerical evaluation. To achieve this, we evaluate a specific scalar ten-propagator topology, employing scattering equations and a spiral-contour method. This approach enables us to derive a precise numerical result, thereby contributing to the broader understanding of N^4SYM and setting the stage for analogous computations in QCD.

Within the topological Rashba Hubbard model, where parent systems fall under non-trivial topological phases, we found that adding spin-orbit coupling to the attractive Hubbard model at half-filling can lead to a topological superfluid state with spin-singlet symmetry, even in the presence of significant spin-flip interactions. This mechanism is vital for creating conventional superfluids suitable for pairing with magnetic quantum solids. We mapped the relationship between these two competing order parameters in a 2D lattice and demonstrated that magnetic order can be nested within non-Abelian Ising topological superfluidity at certain fillings, where it coexists with the required spin-mixture. Additionally, we observed that stronger Hubbard U values lead to a nested magnetic order that weakens as U increases and may switch to double occupancy, limiting its applicability in this context.

By combining terahertz spectroscopy and x-ray diffraction, we have discovered a previously unknown phase transition in a copper oxide superconductor, YBCO. As the material cools from its critical temperature of 92 K, this internal shift creates a symmetric lattice structure with hexagonal symmetry.

The behavior of polymer brushes has long fascinated researchers due to its rich dynamics and diverse applications, particularly with the ability to confine particles within a two-dimensional plane. This work undertakes both theoretical and experimental investigations into disordered polymer brushes composed of elongated rods, filling a gap in understanding their structure by employing high-speed microscopy on visually opaquely samples. It shows that the 'exclusion region', disallowing rotation of embedded particles, shrinks to approximately one rod length in thickness near a surface, and expands into the bulk as the density of rods increases, effectively transitioning from a 2D to a 3D system. This research reveals a missing component in previous studies of active polymer brushes, providing the necessary description of their boundary regions.

Given a graph G and a subset S of its vertices, we say S is a resolving set if for any pair of distinct vertices x and y, the path lengths from x to elements of S differ from the path lengths from y to the elements of S. The minimum size of a resolving set is called the metric dimension of G. Now we say a subset S' of S is a shortened metric basis for G if it is the smallest possible subset of S that remains a resolving set for G. The research we report here is about the properties and characteristics of these minimal subsets.

Recent research utilizing the data from the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope has produced comprehensive all-sky maps, which can be adapted for a wide range of astronomical applications. However, generating these maps of optimal quality is complicated by issues of signal detection across different energy bands and statistical inconsistencies. We are exploring the potential of utilizing suboptimal single-band maps as training data for a neural network model, with the goal of producing a refined all-sky map. Our findings suggest that this approach can significantly enhance maps of moderate quality, although it appears that a neural network model is incapable of compensating for issues arising from mapping variable sources.

A new mechanism for assigning goods has been created, which is more efficient than a serial dictatorship system yet completely decentralized. This means it relies on no pre-set information about the Decentralized Efficiency (DE) of the system. Unfortunately, the mechanism requires the participants to report their true preferences, which is the main limitation.

We analyzed 12 main-belt asteroids from the Pan-STARRS1PS1 Medium Survey, identifying 6 binary systems and 4 potential binaries among them. Through astrometric analysis, we calculated the semi-major axis and orientation of the binaries, and by size analysis, we estimated the semi-major axis in kilometers. Notably, 5 of these asteroids have never been previously confirmed as binary systems, and 2 are, for the first time, recorded as possessing moons. Notably, the record for the smallest known moon of an asteroid is broken, with 2014 SU25's moon having a perihelion distance of 0.118 kilometers. We utilized color analysis to infer the surface albedo of the asteroids, and discovered that 2014 SU25's moon shares a similar albedo to its parent asteroid. Our findings are made available in the public domain, with all data openly accessible on the repository known as Zenodo.

This research outlines and assesses a novel, adaptive regression model for analyzing data from computer networks. We employ network information to correctly specify the model's structure, utilize the model for inferring cause-and-effect relationships, and leverage a specific method to analyze peer influence within networks based on the LASSO estimator. Our assumptions are minimal, utilizing only weak convergence conditions for the network as it grows larger. Our proposed estimator achieves an optimal rate of convergence for the main parameters and a near-optimal rate for the secondary parameters, under the framework of sparse true models.

Our work extends previous studies on peer influence by allowing for a broader class of parameters, including those that are not necessarily sparse, and for which the traditional LASSO estimator does not converge at the optimal rate. This research also establishes a theoretical framework for evaluating the performance of the model and introduces methods for constructing confidence and prediction intervals with reliable coverage rates. Furthermore, it provides criteria for model selection that take into account the complexity of the model.

Multiple simulation experiments demonstrate the model's reliability under various scenarios. A real-world dataset from the network of universities is used to demonstrate the model's ability to identify, assess, and evaluate peer influence among institutions. This case study highlights the model's efficacy in providing accurate and nuanced insights.

This study introduces novel formulations for the Variable-Order Riemann-Liouville Variable-Order differential operator in relation to the Variable-Order Riemann-Liouville Variable-Order integral operator, resulting in a revised Leibniz theorem.

Radio-loud objects like active galactic nuclei and star-forming regions emit strong radio signals across the electromagnetic spectrum, making various wavelength bands useful for studying them. To study these celestial bodies effectively, it's crucial to minimize the impact of the foreground signal from the Milky Way by using advanced telescopes with precise calibration and a understanding of how the foreground signal behaves. In this paper, we develop a series of mathematical models that explain the precision with which next-generation telescopes, such as ALMA and SKA, can detect the structured signals in the sky, and sketched out the steps and necessary conditions to distinguish these signals from the noise using spectral methods and machine learning algorithms.

To facilitate the development of sophisticated algorithms, researchers require user-friendly visualization tools to effectively inspect data images and spectra. This requirement is particularly acute in the fields of astronomy and planetary science, where large data sets are being analyzed using machine learning and where visualization can significantly streamline feature engineering. To enhance the open-source machine learning community, we've created the 2D/3D visualizer and the spectrum editor—two user-modifiable web applications that provide rapid, high-quality visualization of images and editing of spectra directly in a web browser. These tools are built using open-source technologies including Vue.js, D3.js, and Django, leveraging efficient image processing capabilities of web graphics interfaces. The visualizer and the spectrum editor are accessible online via the following URL: https://astro.astroaztec.uaz.edu.mx/.

The Southern Atlantic Ocean's formation is attributed to a central Atlantic rift, specifically in its southern portion, where regional stress conversion from extensional to compressional forces is thought to have facilitated the development of the Natal fracture zone in Brazil, based on previous hypotheses. Contrary to this understanding, detailed analysis of available data indicates that the stress field in this region is characterized by a dominant extensional character. The estimated maximum shear stress is found to be minimal, closely resembling the minimum values typically discovered in mid-ocean ridges. The neutral stress field is determined to be the most suitable model that minimizes overall stress deviations, indicating that the Natal fracture zone likely resulted from the cumulative effects of normal and oblique normal faults formed during the early stages of the South Atlantic's formation.

Information optimization theory has proven useful in computer vision tasks like image classification and has been applied in variousassisted healthcare technologies. This study integrates segmentation part probabilities from self-supervised network outputs and applies information theory concepts to create an objective function that guides network learning without needing paired training data. To enhance efficiency and avoid local minima, we also incorporate a fast approximation method for calculating mutual information and initialize parameters using supervised techniques. Experimental results on public datasets show that our approach performs on par with other self-supervised methods and achieves excellent performance in supervised settings and medical image diagnosis tasks.

We introduce the first system designed to assist and guide a Dungeons and Dragons (DnD) Game Master, a task we call a DnD Game Master Agent (GMA). This first prototype is built on top of a Transformer-based language model, but we demonstrate that simply using a powerful language model is not enough. To effectively guide a play session, the system needs to communicate and make decisions based on the game's progress. Therefore, we suggest a framework where the system learns specific aspects of its behavior based on intent and mindset. This approach results in a system that performs better than one that relies solely on a high-powered language model. We also discuss key components for a GMA, available datasets, and potential future applications.

Despite significant progress, lexico-semantic relationship classification remains a challenging task due to the vast number of possible classifications. To address this issue, many studies focus on a more granular set of categories, such as NYT's 20 news classifications. However, many other classifications, outside of news, are difficult to achieve. This study returns to a broader range ofLEXGLUE's 20 tasks, covering both semantic invariance and semantic change. We propose a distinct set of binary classifications designed to capture a comprehensive range of types of semantic transformations, based on a detailed analysis of existing relationships. Equipped with this new classification framework, we identify significant limitations of current models due to their sensitivity to specific types of embeddings, training data, and semantic changes that they struggle to handle. Furthermore, this study presents a significant advancement in Lexical Semantic Classification by presenting the first model that exceeds human performance.

Investigating the transverse momentum dependence of quark and gluon parton distribution functions (PDFs) is an essential aspect of modern particle physics research. A new set of findings regarding the dependence of these functions on transverse momentum has been recently reported, either支持, or contradicting a conjecture made by one of the authors previously. A new relationship, connecting the average transverse momentum dependence of quark PDFs to the intrinsic transverse momentum dependence, has been proposed, and the necessary conditions, including the necessary (quasi)parton distribution expansions, to validate this relationship, have been examined. Additionally, the proposed findings and considerations are related to the overall understanding of (quasi)parton distribution functions.

Researchers have discovered that knotted proteins contain topological features essential for their function and structural integrity. Despite initial beliefs that protein folds occur gradually, molecular dynamics simulations revealed that topological changes during folding happen instantly. This study builds on previous findings, aiming to identify the precise folding paths that lead to specific knot types. To achieve this, the research focuses on minimizing the complexity of the entanglement within the looped sections of the protein in a simulated solvent environment. By doing so, the researchers can pinpoint the bending sequences that transform the protein into distinct knots, such as a 5_2 knot or a 6_1 knot, or result in an untied loop, all within under 100 steps. Notably, the protein structures formed after these bending sequences closely resemble the original design, offering valuable insights into the folding processes of complex, knotted proteins.

By integrating Planck 2018 data from the Planck 2018 2-year dataset, the Planck 2018 1.4 DB and 1.4-year early dark energy (EDE) dataset with Baryon Acoustic Oscillation (BAO) and Baryon Acoustic Oscillation (BAO) data from the Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey (BOSS) 2015 1.4 EDE DR8, a 4-lambda model fit was performed with fits to the Planck 2018 2-year dataset, the Planck 2018 1.4 EDE dataset with BAO data, and Super-NOvA 2020 data. Specifically, a fit to the full Planck 2018 2-year dataset yielded the following parameters: $\Omega_m h^2 = 0.1430^{+0.0022}_{-0.0018}$, $\frac{l_{*}}{1.048} = 2.072^{+0.018}_{-0.017}$, $A_A = 2.997^{+0.041}_{-0.039}$, and $f_\mathcal{E} = 0.044^{+0.0

Building on previous work, this paper extends the definition of symplectic mapping category groups to include deformations allowed through blowups. For a specific collection of homotopy classes from a torus, we define these expanded symplectic mapping category groups. Additionally, we establish connections between the original and expanded groups, and analyze the fundamental structure of the original group, showing it is closely related to the original group through an exact sequence.

This article provides an overview of the instantaneously broken symmetry, a phenomenon found in both relativistic and nonrelativistic quantum theories that have shared characteristics between them. The article delves into various aspects of this phenomenon, including massless pole separable divergences, zero modes in scalar and gauge theories, and its manifestation in nonrelativistic theories such as nonabelian color magnetism, involving instantaneously broken symmetry. The article also discusses possible sources for generating massless pole separable divergences in nonrelativistic quantum field theory.

Current pre-trained models excel at generating single word counterfactuals but struggle with more complex, multi-word interventions. To address this limitation, we introduce a comprehensive dataset and evaluation protocol for assessing counterfactual generation models' capabilities with multi-word interventions. Specifically, we extract a dataset of 10,000 counterfactuals by leveraging extensive GPT-3 access, covering various settings and interventions. Furthermore, our experiments reveal that even the best existing models perform significantly below human potential, giving non-counterfactual outputs 66% of the time, 34% of the time generating unrelated text.  These results indicate there is substantial potential for improvement in models' capacity to generate coherent and relevant counterfactuals.

The concept of a total colorings method is introduced, which ensures that colored neighbors of any given vertex can be distinguished by combining the colors of adjacent vertices and edges. A specific type of edge-reachable coloring known as a sum distinguishing total coloring is defined. Additionally, two types of sum distinguishing total colorings, the community and fair varieties, are described as subsets of Edges-Reachable colorings that incorporate these distinguishing characteristics within specific communities or among all vertices in a graph. Although numerous studies have been conducted on the conditions for graphs to meet the requirements of a sum distinguishing total coloring, researchers have yet to explore the conditions for graphs to admit community or fair sum distinguishing total colorings. This study introduces the notion of community and fair sum distinguishing total coloring and presents schemes for rendering graphs 'all-encompassing' in these aspects, specifically focusing on certain types of circulant graphs.

In our analysis of ultrathin Heusler films on sapphire through high-resolution transmission electron microscopy, we found that while most layers follow a van der Waals epitaxy, one layer forms a pinhole epitaxy, creating an odd sequence in the structure. A theoretical tight-binding model indicates this unique arrangement arises when middle layers reach critical thickness for switching from van der Waals to distant epitaxy. As the middle layer thickens, it forces adjacent outer layers to reorganize, potentiallyHeusler structure transitions. This alternation, however, occurs at much longer lengthscales. Precise epitaxial patterning of Heusler layers, as suggested, holds the key to controlling the Heusler/Heusler interfaces within the same crystallographic structure.
This paper investigates the structure of rank and null space for $\mathbb{Z}_p\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$-linear codes, where the length of the code is defined as $p^3(p^2-1)$.

A novel approach is presented for enhancing oil recovery, using a hybrid flow pattern that combines longitudinal ideals polymer flukes in the main pipeline with random polymer distribution in side pipelines. This method addresses limitations of existing techniques, such as channeling and bypassing, by providing more effective polymer dispersion within the reservoir while minimizing wall sliding issues. The effectiveness of this concept is evaluated through the use of 3D大尺度 models that simulate the flow of polymer in a sample oil reservoir, demonstrating an increase in oil production output and reduction in channeling depth when compared to traditional injection methods.

The primary issue with current multi-object tracking methods utilizing single-label positive samples is that they struggle to manage situations where a single object displays multiple labels or one label corresponds to more than one object. To address this, we propose a novel approach called Multi-Instance Extraction from Single-Label Samples (MISES), which effectively extracts multi-label instances from these individual label-defining samples. First, we employ a loss function targeting soft IoU to identify high-proportion regions within positively labeled samples that closely match the desired target. Then, we determine whether the extracted regions are distinct, separate objects or parts of a singular entity with a connected structure, which are then treated as positive training data for our model. To effectively train our model, we establish a line of reasoning proving that a combination of soft IoU and an existing model's requirements is sufficient to accurately classify objects during inference, which is also utilized as a constraint for optimizing our loss function to ensure the extracted objects possess sufficient detail to be classified correctly. Ultimately, our approach demonstrates remarkable performance gains over existing models in multi-objective tasks on the MOT16 and DMCP benchmarks, achieving a significant improvement of 28.5% in HOS and 14.1% in DM.

For a time-fractional phase-field equation, an upper energy bound is defined as the sum of the spatial L2 norm of the derivative term, a symmetric matrix multiplier, a time-fractional Caputo derivative term, and the Fenchel conjugate of the potential function. The upper energy bound exhibits monotonic decrease over time for noninitial time points. A corresponding result is established for a non symmetric matrix. The paper also derives parabolic scaling invariance and an energy dissipation equality for the time-fractional phase-field equation.

The relationship between physical systems and their mathematical descriptions is central to scientific methodology, with observables being used to make predictions about a system and then compared to actual observations. A novel form of abstract prediction arises through the study of relationships between systems, with a mathematical structure known as a presentable infinity pre-topos serving as the foundation. This foundation encompasses notions of universal properties, existential quantification, and inclusion, providing a base for understanding the relational aspect. Through an abstract adjunction, we establish a comprehensive framework that includes Hilbert space and the state of a quantum mechanical system as its outcome.

We propose a new theory explaining high-energy gamma-rays found in the energy range of 0.1-3 GeV from the central areas of a variety of nearby low-energy radio galaxies and active galaxies. This includes galaxies like Mkn 2, Mkn 5, Mkn 7, Mkn 9, Mkn 10, Mkn 12, Mkn 16, Mkn 26, Mkn 32, NGC 1275, NGC 4945, and NGC 6264. Existing theories involving a statically charged magnetic disk, previously discussed for some of these galaxies but refined, are now applied to a broader range of galaxies. According to the theory, electrons and ions become trapped in magnetic lines within a rotating, charged disk and accelerate at the points where they cross these lines. Accelerated electrons emit gamma-rays through inverse Commission process, interacting with infrared photons from the disk itself. Calculated results show a good match with actual data, particularly for Mkn 12 and Mkn 16, and can account for all gamma-rays in the observed energy range when considering both Compton process and cosmic-ray interactions with the disk.

This document proposes using the width of the distribution of asset returns, 
referred to as dispersion, in place of variance in mean-variance optimization. 
We develop a new approach to capture dispersion through a linear quadratic 
function of returns and demonstrate its effectiveness through various 
applications, particularly in creating investment portfolios. The proposed 
method is straightforward to understand and implements through a quadratic 
objective function, taking into account both variance and dispersion. 
Compared to traditional methods, our approach offers significant benefits in 
terms of reducing portfolio dispersion and achieving more symmetric return 
distributions. The numerical results show that the proposed approach outperforms 
alternative methods in both risk and return metrics. The results indicate that 
using dispersion leads to more realistic and balanced portfolio outcomes.

This work aims to enhance the performance of Sound Categorization Networks (SCN) in distinguishing normal and abnormal heart sounds, taking into consideration noise, deformation, and various cardiac pathologies. To achieve this, a novel network architecture was proposed which employs a dual-input, dual-output structure combining Sound Categorization Network (SCN) and Sound Reconstruction Network (SRN). The SRN component, utilizing Convolution-Bayes Convolution (CBC) blocks, enhances performance by mitigating noise and deformation effects. Furthermore, a Noise Reduction Module (NRM) is proposed to further enhance heart sound signal quality. The proposed SCN-Bayes demonstrates superior performance in classification tasks, particularly in cases of normal and mixed anomaly classification. Additionally, the proposed NRM and SRN components can be used independently to yield performance improvements.

The healthcare industry can significantly benefit from wearable technology by utilizing collected health data. However, training deep neural network models using this data from multiple sources can lead to inaccuracies due to data heterogeneity. A federated learning approach has emerged as a promising methodology, allowing multiple datasets to collaborate without sharing data externally, while preserving privacy. Despite limitations in existing methods regarding communication efficiency and the negative impact of data diversity on model performance, we introduce a federated transfer knowledge structure, FedHealth, which optimizes the collection of necessary knowledge points for specific service demands, minimizes redundancy, and facilitates the transfer of collective knowledge from participant devices to a virtual server, thereby enhancing model accuracy and efficiency. Experimental results indicate that FedHealth achieves high accuracy and efficiency in real-world wearable healthcare scenarios.

This paper belongs to the technical framework of mathematical finance, specifically addressing the issue of optimizing investment portfolios. We provide an overview of advanced methods that enhance basic Modern Portfolio Theory, focusing on incorporating higher-order moments and comparing them with alternative approaches like robust optimization, efficient frontier expansion, and satisficing theory. We conclude by highlighting directions for future research.

From a string-theoretic perspective, we examine the coincidence problem, a major issue with the standard cosmological model. We argue that the accelerated expansion of the universe's early phases was likely caused by the early universe's vacuum fluctuating as compact scalar fields moved between stable torsion states. Furthermore, we propose that the standard model's particles were the result of torsion states that were close in energy, raising questions about the nature of the particles' fields, masses, and interactions.

This paper presents a system called SAS2, which is designed to automate semi-structured information extraction from academic proceedings. It specifically targets Computer Science topics. As far as we know, this is the third automated review system for selected transaction papers in this field. We invite other review areas to adopt and adapt our system.

In optimal control theory, a key problem arises when trying to toggle a system between two states with minimal cost, particularly when the cost function experiences sudden changes. This paper aims to address this shortcoming by providing a more rigorous proof for the existence of a solution to an optimal control problem where the system can toggle states, but the cost function behaves in a way that precludes the solution from being absolutely continuous. To overcome this limitation, the author proposes an alternative model where the cost function measures the system's states and control inputs at specific time intervals, resulting in a well-defined optimization problem with a continuous objective function.

This paper explores a scenario where two types of leptoquarks, denoted as $S_1$ and $G_2$, are produced and decay in various ways, potentially solving the anomaly found in $g-2$ for both muons and electrons. Despite being a colorful source of baryon asymmetry, the leptoquarks could still be consistent with current particle physics findings if certain conditions are met, such as creating an uneven distribution of matter at the Large Hadron Collider. A table of current constraints from different experiments is provided, illustrating the minimum mass required for the leptoquarks to remain compatible with observed data.

Simple neural network models with limited number of parameters can offer a practical tool for life scientists to analyze and learn patterns in temporal data series, by allowing for the preservation of original dataset dimensions and minimal exposure to large data volumes. Despite being conceptually straightforward, these models often require a more nuanced approach due to their limited learning capabilities. We explore an optimization strategy that integrates life scientists' domain knowledge and data insights, effectively adapting the model to specific application needs and performance requirements. We demonstrate the practical effectiveness of our approach in three scenarios: processing and interpreting gene expression patterns, improving forecast precision, and predicting event occurrences, or alternatives, with expert input and automated adjustments.

We have developed a theoretical model that explains the low-temperature excitation of fine structure lines for certain atomic components like [C~{\sc ii}] 158$\mu$m, C~{\sc i} 82$\mu$m, and 47$\mu$m, and [O~{\sc iii}] 52$\mu$m. Our model is based on radiative transfer and R~{\sc ather] processes within cool gas clouds illuminated by a low-intensity UV radiation from dust. We found that subthermal excitation significantly impacts low-energy transitions, particularly for C~{\sc i} lines, and cannot be neglected when using molecular gas tracers like CO. We discussed how this phenomenon affects estimates of metallicity, gas properties, and carbon sublimation rates, and highlighted the need for models that include multiple metal species for an accurate understanding of these processes. We also revealed that [C~{\sc ii}] line emission mostly originates from gas clouds cooled by a UV radiation field, which comprise a small fraction of the total H~{\sc i} gas reservoir. Since this reservoir is directly probed by [C~{\sc ii}] line emission at a similar wavelength as CO lines, it may be possible to observe two distinct CO components, each corresponding to different gas temperatures.

Within the framework of a composite vector-like model, we investigate the impact of electroweak anomalies on fermions at a scale of few TeV. The model's massless components do not interfere with Standard Model gauge symmetry, yet it allows for a detailed prediction of the expected outcomes from Large Hadron Collider (LHC) searches. In contrast to previous theories, where the anomalous interactions and neutral current interactions were incompatible, our analysis suggests that both types of interactions can coexist, providing a stronger case for this type of new physics. Through an analytical study and numerical data, we show how this new physics would present itself in di-lepton final states produced from $pp \to K \to l^+l^-$ and $pp \to B \to l^+l^-$ processes. Further, we contend that the observed discrepancies in muon data might be a result of new physics manifesting through $K$ and $B$ irregularities, although we note that current LHC capabilities are not yet sufficient to fully explore the parameter space in which this scenario would hold true.

Given $m$ observations of $k$-dimensional data points, a common task in series reconstruction is to recover the original order of given dataset $X=\{x_1, \ldots, x_k\}$ that minimizes the expected divergence from $m$ historical observations. This problem can be reduced to series ordering and has applications in scenarios such as restoring corrupted time series. In this work, we focus on reducing the divergence to the Hamming distance and present two essential conditions for optimality. Furthermore, we present a polynomial-time algorithm to achieve 4$\times$-approximate optimality in our framework. We believe this research can serve as a foundation for addressing more complex series reconstruction problems in real-world applications.

In this study, we tackle the challenge of identifying rare musical instruments, also known as musical device recognition. To address this issue, we introduce a novel approach that utilizes a hierarchical framework consisting of two parts: first, we train a controller on a large dataset of common instruments, and then we train a custom class classifier for each instrument in the controller using a large dataset. For instruments that are not included in the controller, we apply a common classifier. This hierarchical approach allows us to work with small datasets of uncommon instruments while still achieving accurate results. We test our method on a large dataset of recorded steel guitar tracks and demonstrate its effectiveness through comprehensive experiments and objective and subjective assessments of the outcomes. Our results show that our hierarchical framework significantly boosts performance compared to other single-classification models, and we make our results and code accessible through a large dataset of musical instruments.

We introduce a comprehensive dataset consisting of academic papers approved for publication, extracting explicit knowledge from a domain-specific area. This collection, designed for advancing research, can aid in creating evaluation metrics for artificial intelligence systems aiming to facilitate and drive research. We also provide a set of preprocessing tools to extract generalizable information from a conference publication, enhancing the efficiency of human researchers in accessing valuable insights.

We employ high-precision Post-Newtonian expansions to generate waveforms from merging eccentric binary systems and examine the accuracy of these calculations using $O(3.5)$ PN radiation reaction. By analyzing the point at which the calculations diverge from the eccentric-orbit-insensitive General Relativity simulations, we examine the accuracy of these high-precision waveforms. As we increase the accuracy of the PN calculations, we observe corresponding decreases in root-mean-square residuals and increases in effective signal-to-noise ratios for Gaussian noise listeners. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of waveforms on detecting Pulsar Timing Array signals and determine that eccentric binary mergers produce distinct features that could be identified, although their abundance needs further confirmation through numerical simulations. By estimating the number of detectable mergers, we observe that even with significant future improvements in radio telescope sensitivity, only a small fraction of binary mergers would be audible, implying that future N-body simulations may not be overly indicative of radio noise detection ability.

To speed up particles in a asymmetric random walk, we modify their hopping rates accordingly, either by increasing or decreasing them based on their velocities. This modified model maintains key properties of the original Asymmetric Simple Exclusive Random Walk, including particles not moving past each other and having multiple possible velocities. By applying a specific transformation to the site-spatial coordinate, we derive an explicit formula for the particle positions at any given time, which can also be used to analyze related models, such as the two-type ASEP and the random-to-top RPR. We obtain results on the long-term behavior, including cluster formations and detailed cluster structures. Our approach provides a unified framework for these outcomes.

Epidemics historically have been studied using various mathematical and statistical models, which are now urgently needed to interpret the ongoing COVID-19 epidemic. This situation highlights the critical role statistics can play in providing immediate insights and long-term forecasting during this global crisis. Despite being outnumbered by infectious diseases in a discipline long divided into separate areas, researchers and institutions are being called upon to collaborate on modeling outbreaks, with success depending on a shared mathematical language and understanding of model implications. This review will explore simple mathematical concepts, model types, and their role in understanding COVID-19's spread, with a focus on bringing together experts in this field to develop unified models that can support public health decisions during the epidemic.

We examine the effects of a Majorana anomaly in a fermionic system, using a generalized version of the Hubbard model. As a result, fermionic excitations at low energy behave like Majorana particles, and we investigate how this fundamentally changes their dynamic and structural properties. Unlike typical boson or fermion systems, majorana particles exhibit unique characteristics, and our study reveals how they are affected by their environment, leading to distinct changes in their quantum state.

Acronyms are abbreviated forms of terms that consist of initial letters from the original word or phrase. They are extensively used in numerous domains, particularly in social media, to save characters and convey a sense of belonging to a community. Unfortunately, their effectiveness is diminished when the referenced term or phrase is not universally understood, or when the source of the acronym is ambiguous. To address this issue our system, named MadDog, employs Natural Language Processing (NLP) to resolve abbreviations into their full forms. MadDog is a web application that provides clarification for acronyms encountered in text messages, utilizing a neural network to generate accurate de-abbreviations or acknowledge the acronym's popularity. The system is supported by a vast dataset of acronym definitions, or can rely on contextual cues if the acronym is relatively new. MadDog's performance has been evaluated through thorough experiments, demonstrating its capability to resolve a significant percentage of acronyms, or at least determine their level of recognizability.

Paired molecules formed from two-spin polar atoms in a single hyperfine state can be substantiated by inducing molecule-atom scattering through a resonant laser, rather than by directly interacting molecule-molecules.  A theoretical model describing this process involves a two-color Spincor field that accounts for atom-electromagnetic interactions and atom-molecule coupling, allowing for a recovery of dimer bound states within an effective Spincor Hamiltonian.  Additionally, a unique, laser-induced three-body process is discovered where a weak dimer can be transformed into two tightly bound diatomic states, mediated by the absorption of a photon.  This phenomenon has implications for understanding the particle-molecule transition.  Furthermore, predictions are made regarding critical parameters and can guide future experimental validation.

To manage DNA storage at a scalable level, sorting long DNA strands into hierarchical bins is an effective strategy. Two key challenges arise: first, accurately determining the hierarchy and cutting DNA accordingly; second, efficiently updating or deleting specific information within the hierarchical system. We address these challenges by developing novel algorithms. For the first challenge, a novel approach is presented that guarantees optimal performance in terms of cuts used, and we test it on realistic parameters; for h=3 and m=10^9, our method assuringly solves the problem with 99.9% success. In addition, we introduce two novel approaches to update or delete data within the hierarchy, and we analyze their performance, finding that our methods outperform existing ones by 1.42 to 2.17 times in terms of external cuts required.

Topological features have significant roles to play in determining physical properties of matter, with recent research also highlighting their potential applications across multiple disciplines. While conventional topological invariants, calculated as integers, offer valuable insights, there exists another class of topologically sensitive phenomena that do not result in discrete values, also known as anomalous topological singularities. These space-filling singularities can appear within momentum space and have the potential to dictate the behavior of particles in various materials, including semimetals, doped silicon, photonic systems, and topological insulators. This review provides an overview of recent studies on these singularities, with a focus on their topological characteristics and potential implementations in photonic and other systems.

A brain tumor is an abnormal growth inside the cranial cavity that can affect a person's thinking, behavior, and overall quality of life. These growths are classified into three main categories: high-grade, low-grade, and benign tumors. Given their malignant nature, tumors require prompt identification and treatment. Due to the complexity of brain imaging analysis, experts often collaborate to assess MRI scans for accurate tumor detection and segmentation. However, not all experts have expertise in this field, making it challenging to efficiently process multiple cases. To address this issue, there's a growing interest in using deep learning techniques to develop automated methods for tumor identification and classification. In this research, we propose a novel deep learning architecture called Multi-Task Focus Directed Network, which can handle both segmentation and classification tasks simultaneously using MRI images. Our proposed method achieves state-of-the-art results on two public datasets, including Brain Tumor Segmentation 2017 and MRIa.

A concept termed "shadow calculation" will be referred to, despite an unclear origin, within the context of inverse problems. The term denotes the efficient determination of highly oscillatory integrals and integrals affected by abrupt changes, which arise in scenarios such as tomography, seismic imaging, and other fields. The idea of shadow calculation will be explored and various existing methods, such as level set integration, generalized monotone integration, and adaptive integration, will be analyzed. The ultimate goal is to achieve an exact result with a computationally feasible effort. The advantages of using shadow calculation are, first and foremost, an exact solution that avoids statistical noise; a significant reduction in computational time, particularly in seismic imaging; and a feasible implementation. The proposed approach is demonstrated with a level set function resulting from the tomographic inverse source problem and a seismic forward operator. The use of differentiable shadow calculation in solving the tomographic inverse problem and differentiable generalized monotone integration in seismic imaging are also investigated. Moreover, a new implementation of differentiable shadow calculation in Python is introduced and made available online.

A cutting-edge system called Live Deep Video Deinterlacing is pitched for integration in the CVPR 2017 conference, utilizing advanced computer vision technology. The proposed project surpasses conventional interlace processing methods, taking full advantage of state-of-the-art deep learning models. The system utilizes an innovative framework consisting of three distinct modules, with each serving a specific function. The initial module extracts high-quality field data from slightly degraded interlaced field images, resulting in complete pixel-level resolution images for both previous and current frames. A direct interpolation method then seamlessly fills any remaining gaps, utilizing the two reconstructed fields to produce smooth output, with options for either real-time implementation or post-processing enhancement, yielding up to 50% PSNR improvement. The system is built upon three independently developed components, with each employing innovative techniques and configurations, with the deinterlacer employing a customized Convolutional Neural Network, with 50 million parameters, trained live on a GPU using the Live Super-Resolution protocol.

The relationship between the root mean square radii of the neutron distribution in a deformed nucleus at the semi-classical, non-relativistic mean field and semi-classical relativistic mean field levels has been investigated. Investigating these relationships in framework models has been in our study, where we evaluated the neutron distribution in a shape-deformed nucleus in both non-relativistic mean field and relativistic mean field frameworks. Further investigation involved comparing results from our models with experimental data for isotopes of Nd, Sm, Sm, Gd, Dy, Er, Yb and Pb. Additionally, we identified specific SPRF values where the neutron distribution in a relativistic mean field framework matches its non-relativistic counterpart.

Precise and efficient river flow velocity predictions are made possible by the shallow water equations, though they can be challenging to solve due to the vast size and complex geometry of river domains. One approach to obtaining highly accurate flow velocity fields involves introducing artificial boundaries and using pore-scale modeling methods, albeit at a considerable computational cost. This study presents an innovative framework that utilizes deep neural networks to rapidly obtain flow velocities in large river basins. Firstly, a compact dataset is created from pore-scale simulations and fitted to the river shape, and a graph-based deep learning model is trained to generalize predictions to new datasets. We successfully applied this algorithm to the Meuse river and made unexpected flow velocity field discoveries.

Individual photographs captured at various exposure levels within a set of frames are seamlessly blended together to create a single high-dynamic-range (HDR) image that preserves both shadow and highlight details normally lost in ordinary images. A key challenge in this process lies in automatically deciding on the exposure-time settings required for successful frame fusion, typically simplified in previous studies by offering users manual control over these settings. However, this study introduces a fully automatic system that not only determines the optimal exposure times for a pre-determined set of frames but also refines their levels within shadows and highlights to produce a balanced and detailed final image. This algorithm is capable of generating complex HDR photographs inside split-second timeframes on mobile devices without user input.

Causal neural networks are becoming significant in various fields such as medicine, economics, and psychology due to their ability to generalize well and provide reliable insights. However, despite their potential, the causal neural literature lacks a thorough overview. This paper aims to contribute by classifying common tasks within causal neural learning and researching the commonly used methods to solve them. By incorporating references from the current state of the art research, this work serves as an introductory survey for those interested in advancing their knowledge in the realm of causal neural learning.

This study presents findings from an in-depth investigation using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to monitor and analyze the three-dimensional temperature distribution within a gas-solid fluidized bed. The experiments were conducted in the presence of a 7-Tesla vertical magnet, where the temperatures were determined from changes in the apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) maps. To ensure the fluidization bed remained stable under the influence of the magnet, a specially designed fluidized bed reactor was utilized. The reactor allowed for continuous circulation of heat and observation of temperatures in real-time. The results demonstrated excellent accuracy when compared to externally measured temperatures, with a maximal discrepancy of 4.5 Kelvin. Furthermore, the study highlighted the potential of MRI as a reliable non-invasive tool for obtaining high-resolution 3D temperature distributions in fluidization beds and other gas-solid systems.

In algebraic geometry, the principle of boundedness is crucial for constructing moduli spaces, but a significant issue arises because many geometric objects within this field are now studied up to isomorphism. This equivalence relation, typically an adjoint form of a finite group, can lead to non-proper behaviors and singularities, thereby compromising the structural integrity of a moduli space. Our objective is to investigate the underlying causes of these flaws, with a focus on understanding their fundamental nature. As an illustrative case, we examine the coarse moduli space of stable elliptic curves with specified j-invariants, which, for the value -3, exhibits a notable discontinuity. This example is particularly significant due to its ability to reveal insights into the mechanism behind this breach of the expected principle, with implications that may be generalizable to more complex scenarios.

Heart mechanics research faces complex challenges with many underlying variables and often incomplete knowledge, making experimental data interpretation difficult due to inconsistencies from non-uniform data. To address this, a hidden variable may need to be inferred to improve data understanding, though traditional optimization methods struggle with data problems at this scale and are sensitive to local solutions. Our research evaluates the efficacy of optimizing a multilevel system on a coarse grid to reduce the problem's sensitivity and accelerate convergence, and compares this approach to other methods including multigrid, in the context of cardiac mechanics. Results show the best approach combines traditional and multilevel methods, leading to substantial computational time reductions, though further improvements are achieved with the use of the Geometric Multigrid method.

A novel class of random matrix models has been introduced, characterized by independent and identically distributed matrix entries, for which precise formulas are derived for the joint probability distribution of eigenvalues, especially in the case of beta ensembles. The formulas are expressed in terms of effective parameters and modifications of polynomial ensembles, facilitating the derivation of large-N asymptotic behaviors through existing techniques. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that numerous higher-level integral transforms, such as the Airy and Pearcey integrals, arise as boundary behaviors of these polynomial ensemble orthogonal polynomials. Notably, our parameters show a direct correlation with the original beta parameters, implying the occurrence of universality within this framework.

The rapid advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is making significant inroads into the video production industry, which has been characterized by high costs, technical complexities, and extensive time commitments. Thanks to AI technology, content creators can now capture, edit, and manipulate audio-video content more efficiently, resulting in a broader range of applications in fields such as meeting summarization, program editing, fault diagnosis, and sign language interpretation. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of AI-driven video creation techniques and their applications, which are intended to be a resourceful resource for researchers and practitioners in this field. Key issues and potential future directions are also discussed in this review.

Recent advancements in visual question answering systems have achieved remarkable success, yet they primarily focus on accurate questions. In contrast, generating false-looking answers that can fool these AI models has received little attention. We aim to investigate the false sense of security in the field of visual question answering by introducing the first dataset specifically designed for this purpose, called FakeData. Unlike existing VQA datasets, the answers in the training and evaluation sets of our new dataset are completely unrelated to the images, making them entirely random and baseless. As a result, a basic random answer system outperforms several prominent visual question answering models on both the training and evaluation data of our new dataset. Our findings surprisingly show that some of these advanced models often perform at the level of these simplistic random answer systems. Consequently, our new dataset enables researchers to accurately measure the minimum possible error rate for visual question answering models and exposes their unfortunate false sense of security.

To investigate novel acoustic phenomena, particularly microacoustic phenomena, researchers must design and build structures with dimensions measured in micrometers.  However, conventional manufacturing techniques have limitations in producing such highly scaled microstructures, hindering progress.  As research moves towards even smaller structures and higher frequencies, overcoming the constraints of traditional manufacturing becomes crucial for significant breakthroughs.  In this research, we present a method of creating complex, sub-wavelength structures deep inside acoustic material via two-photon lithography, and demonstrate their unique properties by simulating and measuring results.  Firstly, we present a method of generating unusual acoustic waves, and secondly, we present a device capable of manipulating the spin of acoustic waves, enabling the creation of topological edge modes and anomalous acoustic resonances.

In this work, we examine how particles diffuse anomalously through random networks,  
where the nodes are connected by links with varying permeabilities. Particles experience  
a "trap-mediated subdiffusion" as they move between nodes, but exhibit "Grassian diffusive  
behavior" when considering their displacement relative to the one-dimensional diffusion.  
Our analysis reveals that the long-term survival of particles is governed by the more  
extreme values of permeability, which can be modeled using the Gumbel distribution.

A first-principles, classical theory is developed to utilize the Gaussian envelope approximation in modeling the electric displacement field for linear and Kerr-nonlinear waveguide-resonator modes, assuming slow temporal and spatial variations. Resonator and waveguide modes are modeled using a one-dimensional theory, and a model is created that extends the linear model to include Kerr nonlinearity. Key effects such as phase and frequency shifts, and the Kerr effect in time, are examined within this generalized framework. Furthermore, a resonator-driven, parametric process is analyzed and modeled, leading to a novel equation and one application demonstrated with a dielectric-filled resonator and plane-wave-like waveguide modes.

Modern control systems frequently employ controls that are limited in magnitude.  However, systems with controls that are not limited often appear in theoretical analyses and theoretical frameworks.  For example, controls that are not limited are a standard assumption in control theory research involving stabilizing control laws that are linear.  Despite their utility, these examples create a paradox, as no stabilizing control law exists for systems with controls that are not limited in certain scenarios, although limited controls can stabilize the same system.  To address this issue, we introduce a novel approach, stable convergence, which allows for stable systems with controls that are not limited, as long as controls within a certain range achieve stable convergence.  To demonstrate this concept, we introduce two new theorems, stable convergence Lyapunov theorems and input-to-state stability Lyapunov theorems, which provide system descriptions that correspond to stable convergence and input-to-state stability, respectively, using limits as controls approach infinity.  In contrast, traditional stability definitions, like local asymptotic stability, do not make sense in the context of controls that are not limited.

A researchers team investigated the characteristics of a chaotic flow around a circular cylinder at various Reynolds numbers, specifically focusing on flow details that are highly sensitive to small changes, making them difficult to observe with large measurement grids. To obtain a more precise understanding of flow behavior, they enhanced the spatial resolution of their available measurement data, utilizing a machine learning approach called generative adversarial networks. This method enabled them to recover a more comprehensive flow picture, including fine flow features, from limited measurement data, around the cylinder, in its wake, and in its boundary layer, at Reynolds numbers of 40, 65, and 100. Two machine learning models, edge-refining GAN and volume-refining GAN, were developed and evaluated, with the former yielding more accurate results, improving $C_\mathrm{D}$ values by 2-3 times and $C_\mathrm{L}$ values by 1.5 times, in comparison to traditional simulation models.

The study examines the properties of the wave equation, specifically focusing on time-independent scenarios, within quantum mechanics. It demonstrates that the probability associated with a system described by the given wave equation remains unchanged over time, provided the potential function is real. Additionally, the research establishes that, for a given kinetic and potential energy, the total energy attains an extreme value when the potential function relies on a real parameter, under the condition that the system's state remains unchanged. It is also inferred that systems with identical kinetic energy and the same potential function, evaluated at corresponding points, will exhibit frequencies that satisfy a specific equality.

Current multi-agent systems, such as those used in automotive applications, are limited by closure-world assumptions and extensive state-space searches, which do not reflect real-world conditions. These systems often struggle to identify and track new objects and tend to overestimate their certainty. This paper introduces a novel, energy-based, probability-like ambiguity model that is fully factorizable, efficiently computable, and provides a clear certainty bound. By integrating this model, we are able to present an open-world tracking approach that successfully detects, distinguishes, and follows objects using a minimal set of sensor data. Our experiments across multiple scenarios show substantial reductions in uncertainty, surpassing traditional ambiguity models and outperforming current open-world tracking methods. Furthermore, our approach is able to decrease operational uncertainty by more than half, exceeding the initial预设 and ensuring safety within expected limits.

Deep reinforcement learning techniques have been successfully applied to numerous complex real-world optimization issues, including network management and scheduling tasks. To evaluate these algorithms under realistic conditions, we have developed L2Explorer, a comprehensive framework that provides a range of pre-configured testing scenarios and features. L2Explorer includes the capabilities to generate log files, modify network parameters, and ensure reproducibility through containerization. Furthermore, we have conducted a pilot study to assess the performance of two reinforcement learning algorithms, L2QL and L2CQL, on real-world 5G backhaul scheduling tasks. The results showed that L2QL achieved an 11.55% improvement in spectral efficiency compared to existing greedy algorithms, and L2CQL further enhanced this result to 13.71%. The source code and configurations for L2Explorer are freely accessible on GitHub.

The timing and frequency of process instances can offer valuable insights in many processes, such as business processes, processes used in manufacturing, and processes monitored within networks. However, existing techniques for analyzing processes mainly focus on the flow of cases, neglecting crucial information about the timing and frequency of process log entries that could be exploited for real-time process monitoring, diagnosis, and iterative process improvement. This paper addresses this gap by introducing a new approach to analyzing and monitoring processes in declarative networks, using mathematical structures known as timed and time-enabled petri nets, and developing an algorithm for process refinement based on a stream of data. This proposed approach is shown to be effective through its application in analyzing processes in computer networks, with demonstrated results in a comparative study and successful integration of cases and timing metrics in subsequent processes.

In one-dimensional quasiperiodic structures, transition points where quasi-bound states become extended have been studied widely. We discovered two novel phenomena occurring at these transitions in photonic quasicrystal waveguide samples, which we then characterize using an effective non-Hermitian model. Specifically, we observe a dual phenomenon: a self-overlapping band structure reversal and a degrading and restoring coupling strength between modes, manifesting as a two-step phase transition. The occurrence of photonic delocalization in one-dimensional quasicrystal systems is found to depend critically on both the strength of coupling and displacement.

Liger, the high-resolution optical spectrograph installed at the W. M. Keck Observatory in 2023, features 6 x 1.0D fibers capable of delivering a total resolution of 450000 and a wide spectral range from 3800 to 10000 Angstroms. This allows it to study various astrophysical phenomena, including elemental abundances, stellar rotation, and binary systems, with great precision. However, processing and analyzing these rich and diverse datasets presents significant challenges, necessitating the development of a robust data processing framework. Liger's data processing system has been designed to overcome these challenges and overcome limitations imposed by software restrictions within the W. M. Keck Observatory environment, ensuring a seamless data processing and workflow at an optimal cost.

Optical demultiplexing using spatial modes is crucial in quantum information processing, and recently, bi-photon entangled states were proposed to achieve high-resolution fractionally sub-Hansens sampling. However, the experiment was constrained by low detection efficiency. In this work, we introduce an efficient method to experimentally analyze the spatial distribution of photons by utilizing two single-photon detectors and a spatial mode converter, which allows us to identify the resolved structure directly from measured data without relying on coincidental detections. Furthermore, this method enables the direct observation of resolved details, such as the Grating and Rayleigh lines, and demonstrates a significant reduction in the minimum resolvable distance. Additionally, we prove that this efficient approach maintains the enhanced super-resolution capability.

The primary goal of this project is to bridge the gap between the algebraic and analytic understandings of compactifications for vector spaces and orthogonal direct sums of vector spaces over a field, especially when considering their respective generalizations. This particular aspect is explored with emphasis on completing a key problem addressed by Borger in his work on the analytic and algebraic Grassmannians, as presented in his 2010 thesis.

The dynamics of an ecosystem depend on its species' behavioral timescales, which can lead to unexpected early warnings of significant demographic changes, especially in systems influenced by an additional faster timescale.  
A general mathematical model is created to examine this phenomenon, featuring an ecosystem with two species that interact on different timescales.  
Interestingly, the model predicts that a sudden demographic shift, specifically a bifurcation, is initially signaled by a surprising oscillatory pattern in population data.  
However, this expectation is countered by an actual study of the Galapagos marine ecosystem near Wolf Island, which, when modeled and analyzed, does not exhibit this predictive long-lasting transient behavior.  
Instead, the island's population of rapidly reproducing algae and slowly reproducing sea urchins during an early alert period is found to be effectively damped, which is attributed to a specific mechanism known as the limit cycle contraction effect.  
This phenomenon leads to the anticipated early warning signals taking the form of gradually increasing amplitude fluctuations and a build-up of variance, which ultimately provides a crucial distinction between different types of population dynamics systems.

By associating the star formation rate (SFR) with the magnitude of a galaxy, a linear correlation is observed at low masses but a significant deviation occurs at higher masses. To determine whether this deviation results from the star formation history being influenced by mass independently or if galaxies above a certain mass threshold possess inherent properties that constrain their future star formation capabilities, researchers studied the relationship between specific parameters, including color, magnitude, and the presence of bulges, with the current SFR in both HST and SPITZER wavelength ranges. A crucial finding from this investigation is that to explain the deviation in star formation behavior at higher masses, there must be a significant shift in the relationship between the presence of bulges and galaxy mass. Additionally, to above $\approx 10^{10}M_{\odot}$, there needs to be a corresponding shift in the relationship between the red color of galaxies and their mass. Therefore, in order to above $10^{10}M_{\odot}$, above 50 percent of these galaxies need to possess bulges, and above 1 gigasolar crest, galaxies need to be significantly darker in color.

Emotion recognition, sentiment assessment, and sentiment classification are fundamental aspects of sentiment analysis. Beyond standard single-task training, this paper explores the potential of multi-task learning to enhance sentiment assessment algorithms' generalization and robustness. Building on a previously proposed method that utilizes a sentiment assessment network capable of identifying universal emotions and task-specific classification layers for language-specific tasks, this study extends the approach to a multi-task learning framework. By incorporating a previously published English dataset and conducting additional experiments, the authors demonstrate the efficacy of this extended framework in the context of multi-task learning.

Multi-agent coordination systems, known for effective joint task execution, 
can be seen as a modern-day fence among agents working together. We propose a novel
concept called self-disapproval and self-deprecation rates to evaluate an agent's
ability to stay within this fence. We provide a framework where an agent can
successfully maintain its fence through negotiation, even when subjected to
various forms of exploitation. Our approach uses self-disapproval and self-deprecation
to guide the agent's decision-making process and ensure continued cooperation.

Freiman's 3k-4 conjecture posits that, given a sumset A + B, where |A| = k and |B| = k - 2, the number of sumset elements |A + B| is at least 2k - 1, with the condition that A and K for some field K are independent. We've established that this condition can be relaxed to meet the original conjecture's requirements.

A fundamental question arises regarding the set of functions that represent fractional Brownian motion with a given Hurst parameter, denoted by $H$, conditional on being non-negative at all points in time. Let's denote this set as $\mathbb{B}_+$. Our study proves two significant findings regarding $\mathbb{B}_+$: first, it establishes that the Lebesgue measure of $\mathbb{B}_+$ is greater than zero; second, it demonstrates that $\mathbb{B}_+$ has a non-empty interior. These results are achieved by identifying subsets of $\mathbb{B}_+$ that possess a positive Lebesgue measure and a non-empty interior respectively.

This study combines quantum disorder theory with the H\'enon-Heiles framework to utilize Dirac's successful trial wave function and apply the principle of minimum variation to calculate the H\'enon-Heiles Hamiltonian eigenvalues. By applying the H\'enon-Heiles Hamiltonian to both regular and stochastic quadratic systems, our method effectively calculates its corresponding eigenvalues, demonstrating that the H\'enon-Heiles framework can effectively model systems with various degrees of chaos. Furthermore, this approach is simpler, more straightforward, and computationally less expensive, requiring only the evaluation of the H\'enon-Heiles Hamiltonian's expectation value. As a result, it is a practical and user-friendly method that can be easily applied to calculate the H\'enon-Heiles framework's spectrum.

X-ray images can be classified into three categories based on the possible severity of COVID-19: Normal, Non-COVID-19, and COVID-19.  
This study aims to investigate the differences between Normal, Non-COVID-19, and COVID-19 patients by analyzing their x-ray images.  
We utilized 1,080 images, with 360 images for each category, to study the characteristics of COVID-19 patients.  
To do this, we extracted linear frequency domain features and applied both Linear Discriminant Analysis and Support Vector Machine to analyze the data.  
Our results indicate that the classification accuracy of three-categories is lower than that of two-categories.  
Moreover, our study suggests that the characteristic of COVID-19 patients lies between Normal and Non-COVID-19 patients.  
Specifically, we propose a method to distinguish COVID-19 patients from Normal and Non-COVID-19 patients using a threshold.  
When we set the threshold at 0.5, the classification accuracy of three-categories is 0.724.  
To further investigate, we plan to collect more data and conduct a data augmentation experiment.

We prove that a simplicial bundle, as defined by J.C. Whitehead's foundational theory, is equivalent to a simplicial structure, thereby establishing its compatibility with the theory of simplicial groups. This equivalence provides a equivalence between two theories: a simplicial bundle and a total simplicial set along with a simplicial action map, particularly highlighting that both theory yield identical fundamental group sequences.

Association detection in multimodal learning has gained significant attention due to its intuitive nature and resource efficiency. Nevertheless, conventional association datasets contain numerous inaccuracies, resulting in conventional supervision methods encountering performance bottlenecks. Analysis reveals that the majority of incorrect associations stem from "long-tail" items that appear frequently but have rare co-occurrences and short-term dependencies among video frames and diverse textual descriptions. To address these issues, we introduce a novel, influential loss called TOP-assLoss, aimed at overcoming the issues with data that are easily misclassified as associated. Specifically, we propose a guiding loss that is driven by items with high-frequency appearances and leverages contextual information from cross-modal features to filter out incorrect associations. The experimental outcomes on two distinct datasets, IR-VideoN2T and IR-VideoSearch, demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, leading to substantial improvements when using R-Net as the baseline and also showing gains with the stronger baseline models.

This study introduces an innovative supervised learning framework called Delta Sampling R-BERT, which is particularly effective for action recognition tasks under conditions of limited data. We utilize pre-trained image encoders and a series of backward epochs to efficiently train our classifier. Experimental results show that our method outperforms both conventional and advanced approaches, achieving remarkable accuracy rates of 91.14% on 50-Action recognition dataset and 81.41% on HW action recognition dataset. Furthermore, our classifier demonstrates the ability to accurately recognize actions in a dim-light environment with only 10 training samples per action, achieving 73.11% accuracy rate on 10 basic actions.

Content-addressable computers, first proposed in the 1960s, offer a highly parallel architecture capable of executing thousands of simultaneous operations and has until now only been a theoretical concept.
